0.title: Faith That Works: The Letter of James
0.overview:
James is the most practical book in the New Testament, and one of the most misunderstood. Martin Luther famously called it “an epistle of straw,” contrasting its apparent emphasis on works with Paul’s gospel of grace. He was wrong. He was fighting the Roman Catholic teaching that our works earn merit before God, and in the heat of that fight he read James as a rival to Paul, when the two belong together. Read on its own terms, James is not a rival to the gospel of grace but its most searching ethical application: what does genuine, living, gospel-produced faith actually look like? The answer is not passive and invisible. It looks like patience in trials, generosity to the poor, a bridled tongue, peaceful wisdom, and prayer that moves heaven.

The author identifies himself as “James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ” (1:1). The most natural identification is James the brother of Jesus, the leader of the Jerusalem church, the man who had not believed in Jesus during his earthly ministry (John 7:5) but was transformed by a resurrection appearance (1 Cor 15:7) into the pillar of the first church (Gal 2:9) and its martyred leader (Josephus, Antiquities 20.9). The letter was probably written before the Jerusalem Council of AD 49, making it possibly the earliest New Testament letter. If so, James was wrestling with the application of the gospel to practical life before Paul had written most of his letters.

The letter draws deeply on the Sermon on the Mount, which James had presumably heard from Jesus himself, and on the Old Testament wisdom tradition — Proverbs, Job, the Psalms of lament. It is addressed to “the twelve tribes in the Dispersion” — Jewish Christians scattered beyond Palestine, probably after the persecution that followed Stephen’s martyrdom (Acts 8:1). These were people under pressure: poverty, being pushed to the edges of society, the temptation to compromise, and churches pulling apart under the strain.

James’s relationship to Paul is complementary, not contradictory. Paul says Abraham was justified by faith (Rom 4); James says Abraham was justified by works (Jas 2:21). They are using the word in two settings. Paul speaks of justification before God in the court of heaven: God’s legal verdict of “righteous”, which comes through faith alone. James speaks of being shown righteous before people in visible life: the proof that faith is genuine, which appears in its works. Both agree that dead faith saves no one; both agree that living faith produces fruit. Paul says faith alone justifies; James says the faith that justifies is never alone.

Read James as the letter that will not let you be comfortable with a merely intellectual Christianity. It asks the hardest questions: Does your faith survive under pressure? Does it make you generous? Does it control your tongue? Does it make you humble? Does it make you pray? These are not questions about earning salvation but about whether what you call faith is the real thing. James is not offering a second route to justification; he is describing what justification produces in the life of the one who has genuinely received it. It produces the kind of faith that works, which is the only kind that is faith at all.

1.title: Tested and Proven: Trials, Wisdom, and the Word
1.overview:
Chapter 1 sets out the letter’s concern: real faith under pressure. His readers are in trials, and in God’s hands trials produce what nothing else can: tested faith, steadfastness and maturity.

Three threads run through the chapter: trials and the faith they prove (vv. 2–12); temptation, which comes from our own desires, not from God, the unchanging giver of every good gift (vv. 13–18); and the word of God, which gives new birth, must be done and not only heard, and produces pure religion (vv. 19–27). The key word is “perfect” or “complete” (vv. 4, 17, 25): not flawless, but whole. Its opposite is the double-minded man (v. 8).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–18 — Trials, Wisdom, and the God Who Does Not Change
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: James writes to scattered believers in trials: God uses tested faith to make them mature, gives wisdom to those who ask with an undivided heart, and promises the crown of life. He never tempts anyone; every good gift, above all the new birth, comes from the unchanging Father.
verseByVerse.theology:
Testing and Tempting

God tests to prove and strengthen; he never tempts. Temptation comes from our own desire, while every good gift comes from the Father of lights, who does not change.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The readers were scattered believers under real pressure.

Now: Counting trials joy is a judgment about what they produce, and it can be made while we are still in pain.

verseByVerse.quote: James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, To the twelve tribes in the Dispersion: Greetings.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. James 1 sets out the letter’s great theme: real faith shows itself in a whole, undivided life, under trial, in prayer, in money, against temptation, and in doing the word it has heard.

The setting. The author is almost certainly James the Lord’s brother, who came to faith after the resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:7) and led the Jerusalem church (Acts 15:13–21; Galatians 2:9). Known as James the Just, he was remembered, Eusebius records from the second-century writer Hegesippus, for knees hardened like a camel’s from prayer; Josephus tells how the high priest Ananus had him stoned around AD 62. Many date the letter to the 40s, which would make it perhaps the earliest New Testament book; others place it nearer James’s death. It is full of echoes of the Sermon on the Mount: the brother who once did not believe in him (John 7:5) now writes in his words.

A servant. The word is doulos: slave, a man who belongs to someone else. The writer led the Jerusalem church, was one of the men Paul calls pillars of the church (Galatians 2:9), and was, the New Testament says plainly, the Lord’s brother (Mark 6:3; Galatians 1:19).

The brother who says slave. He grew up in the same house and ate at the same table for perhaps thirty years; in a church that prized connection with Jesus, that claim would have opened every door. He writes “slave”, and never mentions the relationship at all.

The Lord Jesus Christ. Once his brothers came to take him home, because people were saying he was out of his mind (Mark 3:21). What changed is recorded in a single line: “Then he appeared to James” (1 Corinthians 15:7). Now the doubting brother calls him Lord, gives him the title Christ, the promised Messiah, and names him in the same breath as God. The man who knew Jesus longest from the outside came to know him last from the inside, and when he did, he bowed. That is what the risen Christ does with unbelief: he does not argue it away, he appears to it. That line about James belongs to a summary of the gospel which Paul says he received and handed on, and Paul had met James himself (Galatians 1:19), so it is not a legend from a later generation. The resurrection best accounts for a doubting brother who became a leader of the church and died for it.

The twelve tribes in the Dispersion. The Dispersion (scattering) was the name for Jews living outside the land of Israel; here it probably means Jewish Christians living abroad, perhaps including those driven out by the persecution after Stephen’s death (Acts 8:1; 11:19). And James addresses a scattered, frightened, poor collection of believers by the most dignified name in Israel’s history. The church is God’s people scattered as pilgrims in the world (1 Peter 1:1), and nobody in it is a stray.

Greetings. The ordinary salutation of a Greek letter, literally “rejoice”. As a letter greeting it appears elsewhere only in a Roman officer’s letter (Acts 23:26) and in the Jerusalem council’s letter drafted under this man’s presidency (Acts 15:23). And it is a wordplay: the very next word in Greek is joy. James has barely said hello before he is talking about joy, to people under pressure.

Where Christians differ: was James a full brother of Jesus? Roman Catholic teaching holds that Mary remained a virgin all her life, so that the brothers of Jesus were cousins or children of Joseph by an earlier marriage; many Orthodox Christians hold the second view. This commentary’s view: the most natural reading of the New Testament is that James was a younger half-brother of Jesus, a son of Joseph and Mary born after Jesus. Matthew 1:25 says Joseph knew her not until she had given birth to a son, and Jesus is called her firstborn (Luke 2:7). The Gospels name his brothers and mention sisters alongside Mary (Mark 6:3), and the Greek has perfectly good words for cousin which are never used of them. Those who hold the other views point out that brother could be used loosely of relatives, and they hold them out of real honour for Mary; but the doctrine of perpetual virginity is not taught in Scripture. This does not lessen Mary’s honour as the mother of our Lord. All generations call her blessed (Luke 1:48), and the best honour we can give her is to do what she said at Cana: whatever he tells you, do it (John 2:5).

What it does not mean. Addressing the twelve tribes does not mean the letter is only for ethnic Jews; it is Scripture for the whole church, and it has fed Gentile believers for two thousand years.

Which James is this? The New Testament has several. James the son of Zebedee, John’s brother, was one of the Twelve, but Herod had him killed very early, around AD 44 (Acts 12:2), probably too early to have written this letter. James the son of Alphaeus was also one of the Twelve, but nothing else is known of him. The James who could simply sign himself James, with no further description, and expect every church to know who he meant, was the leader of the Jerusalem church, the Lord’s brother. That is why most scholars, and the church from early on, have taken him to be the author.

Should James be in the Bible at all? Luther did call it an epistle of straw, in 1522, comparing it with Romans, Galatians and John, because he found it said too little about Christ and grace and feared it taught justification by works. But Luther kept it in his Bible, though near the end, and preached from it, and his own later followers and the whole Reformed tradition have received it gladly as Scripture. James does not deny justification by faith; he denies that a faith which produces nothing is the faith that justifies, which is exactly what Paul teaches too (Galatians 5:6). Read James as the Spirit’s word to comfortable believers, and the straw turns out to be iron.

In everyday life. Most of us reach for something when we want to be taken seriously: the job title, the qualification, the person we know. James had the best connection in the history of the world and did not use it; belonging to Christ was enough, and it can be enough for you.
verseByVerse.note: James was most likely the brother of Jesus, who came to faith after the resurrection and led the Jerusalem church. He was put to death about AD 62. “The Dispersion” means Jewish believers scattered outside the land of Israel. The letter echoes Jesus’ Sermon on the Mount again and again.

verseByVerse.quote: Count it all joy, my brothers, when you meet trials of various kinds, for you know that the testing of your faith produces steadfastness. And let steadfastness have its full effect, that you may be perfect and complete, lacking in nothing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Count it all joy, my brothers. He does not say “feel joy”. The verb is reckon, consider, an accounting word. James is not commanding an emotion, which nobody can produce on demand, but a judgment about what trials are, and a judgment can be made while you are still miserable. All joy means pure joy: not joy in the pain itself, but in what God is doing through it.

When you meet trials. When, not if. The verb means to fall into, as the man fell among robbers (Luke 10:30). Trials are not scheduled; you come round a corner into them: the phone call, the diagnosis, the letter, the conversation that goes wrong.

Of various kinds. The word is many-coloured, like a woven cloth: poverty, persecution, illness, bereavement, the slow ache of a prayer not yet answered. Peter uses the same word of God’s varied grace (1 Peter 4:10): there is no shade of suffering for which God does not have a matching shade of grace.

Testing produces steadfastness. The joy is not irrational; it is informed. The word for testing is the assayer’s term: the process that proves metal genuine and refines it in the same fire (1 Peter 1:7). And what it produces is hypomonē: not passive resignation but the capacity to remain under a weight without collapsing. It cannot be learned from a book or handed over in answer to a prayer; it grows only while we are actually bearing the weight.

Its full effect. There is a warning folded into that. The process can be cut short: by escaping at any cost, by numbing it, by getting bitter, all of which end the discomfort and end the work with it. James is asking his readers not to walk out of the refiner’s shop while the metal is still in the fire.

Perfect and complete. Perfect here is teleios, meaning finished, having reached its end, not sinless. Complete means whole in every part, with nothing missing. James is describing maturity, and he says the road to it runs through the thing you would most like to avoid.

The road the Son walked first. The maturity James describes is the likeness of a person: God’s purpose is that we be “conformed to the image of his Son” (Romans 8:29). And Christ went this way first: “Although he was a son, he learned obedience through what he suffered. And being made perfect, he became the source of eternal salvation” (Hebrews 5:8–9). He had no sin to be refined away; “made perfect” means fully fitted, through suffering, to be our Saviour. The maturity James promises is his likeness formed in us, by the same road.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we should pretend trials do not hurt, or seek out suffering. Jesus wept at a friend’s tomb and agonised in the garden (John 11:35; Mark 14:33–34); Christian joy is not the absence of tears but something underneath them. Nor does it mean every hardship should simply be accepted. If you can lawfully escape danger, or get treatment, or leave an abusive situation, you should. Endurance is for what God does not remove, not a reason to stay where he has given you a way out.

Does this mean God sent my suffering? Scripture says God rules over all things, including our trials, and that nothing reaches his children except by his permission and for his purpose (Romans 8:28; Lamentations 3:37–38). But he does not delight in our pain, and many trials come through other people’s sin, which he hates. The comfort is not that every hard thing is good in itself. It is that no hard thing is wasted. The same God who allowed Joseph to be sold by his brothers used it to save many lives (Genesis 50:20). You may not see the purpose this side of heaven, and you are not required to. You are invited to trust the one who does.

How can I count it joy when I am crushed or grieving or depressed? Remember the verb: it is reckoning, not feeling. You may weep every day this month and still be counting it joy, if in the middle of the tears you say: “Lord, I do not understand this, but I believe you are working, and I will not let go.” That is what the Psalms do; many of them begin in darkness. If you are depressed, seek help from your doctor and your pastor; that is not a failure of faith. The joy James means is often a quiet thing: a stubborn confidence that God is not finished, held with a trembling hand.

Is this not just positive thinking, or the old Stoic advice to keep a stiff upper lip? No, and the difference is a Person. The Stoic said pain does not really matter, so rise above it; positive thinking says look on the bright side. James says the pain is real and the tears are allowed, but the trial is in the hands of a Father who is using it, and its goal is not that you feel nothing but that you become like his Son (Romans 8:29). Stoic calm rests on your own strength of mind, and breaks when that runs out. Christian joy rests on what God is doing, which is why the weak can have it too.

verseByVerse.quote: If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously to all without reproach, and it will be given him. But let him ask in faith, with no doubting, for the one who doubts is like a wave of the sea that is driven and tossed by the wind.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If any of you lacks wisdom. The connection is the point. James has just said trials produce maturity, “lacking in nothing” (v. 4). The practical problem is that inside a trial you cannot see what it is doing, or what to do next. So he goes on, “If any of you lacks”, using the same word. This is not a general offer of intelligence but wisdom for the trial: how to act in the middle of something you did not choose and cannot understand. Biblical wisdom is skill in living, seeing life from God’s point of view (Proverbs 2:6).

Let him ask God. That is the whole method. Not “work it out”, not “consult the experienced first”, not “wait for clarity”: ask. The verb is a present imperative, and it carries the sense of keep asking. Solomon was offered anything, and asked for an understanding mind to govern God’s people and to discern between good and evil, and God was pleased (1 Kings 3:9–12). The God who answered that prayer has not changed his mind about it.

Without reproach. He gives generously (haplōs): the word means singly, simply, without calculation, holding nothing back, with an open hand and a whole heart. And without reproach, which is the tender one. He does not sigh. He does not remind you that you asked last month, or that you would not need to ask if you had listened the first time. He never tires of being asked. Generous, simple, whole-hearted giving is not something God does occasionally. It is what he is.

And it will be given him. A flat promise, without conditions about how clever you are, and James had first heard it from his brother: “Ask, and it will be given to you”, and “how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him!” (Matthew 7:7–11). And all such wisdom comes from one treasury. Christ Jesus became to us wisdom from God (1 Corinthians 1:30), and in him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Colossians 2:3). To ask for wisdom in a trial is, at bottom, to ask to know Christ in it and to see it as he sees it. The answer may not be a plan. It will be more of him.

Ask in faith. This needs care, because it has wounded people. The doubting described is not the ache of a believer who struggles; the man who said “I believe; help my unbelief!” got what he asked for (Mark 9:24). The word means to be divided, at odds within oneself, debating whether to trust God or rely on something else. To ask in faith is to come trusting God’s character and promise, not your own certainty.

Like a wave of the sea. The image explains it. A wave has no fixed position at all: driven and tossed by the wind, it goes wherever it is pushed. That is a man who wants God’s wisdom on Sunday and the world’s on Monday, who asks and then goes to arrange matters himself. He is not weak in faith. He is in two minds, and the next verses name it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God will give whatever we ask if we only believe hard enough; the promise here is for wisdom, and in all our asking God answers according to his will (1 John 5:14). Faith is not a force we generate to make things happen. It is trust in a Person.

How does God actually give wisdom? Should I expect a voice or a sign? Ordinarily God gives wisdom through his word, which is able to make you wise (2 Timothy 3:15), through a mind being renewed by it (Romans 12:2), through the counsel of mature believers (Proverbs 15:22), and through his providence opening and closing doors. Scripture is complete and sufficient, so we do not need new revelations (Christians who believe God still guides by impressions or prophecy generally agree that any such sense must be tested by Scripture and can never add to it); the Spirit’s work is to help us understand and apply what he has already said. In practice, wisdom often comes quietly: a passage that suddenly fits your situation, a friend’s question, a growing clarity over days. Ask, read, seek counsel, then act on the best light you have, trusting God to correct you if you are wrong.

I asked for wisdom and I still do not know what to do. Sometimes wisdom is not a clear answer about the future but the grace to take the next right step. God may not show you the whole road; he promises a lamp to your feet (Psalm 119:105), which lights one step at a time. If two paths are both lawful and both seem wise, you are free to choose, and God is not waiting to punish you for picking the wrong door. And sometimes the wisdom we lack is not what to do but how to bear what we cannot change, patiently, without bitterness. That is wisdom too, and it is often the deepest answer to this prayer.

verseByVerse.quote: For that person must not suppose that he will receive anything from the Lord; he is a double-minded man, unstable in all his ways.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He is a double-minded man. The word is dipsychos, two-souled, and so far as we can tell James coined it; it appears nowhere in Greek before this letter. He means a man with two centres operating at once, two genuine loyalties pulling in different directions. He prays sincerely and hedges sincerely. The contrast is with God, who gives simply (v. 5): the giver is undivided, and the asker is in two pieces.

The single eye. James learned the contrast from his brother. Jesus said that the healthy eye (literally the single eye, haplous, the word behind God’s generous giving in verse 5) fills the whole body with light, and that no one can serve two masters (Matthew 6:22–24). A heart is made single not by straining to want one thing, but by finding the one Master worth all of it.

The disease of the whole letter. Double-mindedness is the root of everything James will confront: faith without works (2:14), blessing and cursing from one mouth (3:10), friendship with God and with the world (4:4). He uses the word again at 4:8 with the remedy: draw near to God, and purify your hearts, you double-minded. The whole letter is a call to be one person before God.

Unstable in all his ways. Not only in his prayer life; in all his ways. The word means restless, unsettled, and James uses it again of the tongue, a restless evil (3:8). A man divided at the centre is divided everywhere.

Why does such a man receive nothing? Not because God is withholding out of pique. It is nearer to say he is unable to receive: a man who asks for wisdom while intending to keep his options open has not actually asked for it. He has asked for a second opinion, which he will weigh against the others. The searching question this puts is not whether you doubt. It is whether, before you prayed, you had already decided what you would do if the answer went the wrong way.

How do I know whether I am double-minded or simply weak? The weak believer wants God wholly and finds he cannot do it well; the double-minded man wants God partly and is content to keep it that way. The weak believer grieves over his divided heart and brings it to God; the double-minded man has made his peace with it. So ask: is there an area of my life where I have quietly decided God will not have the final word? Money, a relationship, my reputation, a habit? If you find one and it troubles you, that trouble is the Spirit’s work, and it is the first sign of a heart being made whole.

Can a divided heart be made whole? Yes, and God is the one who does it. David prayed: “Unite my heart to fear your name” (Psalm 86:11). God promised his people one heart and a new spirit (Ezekiel 11:19). So start there: pray David’s prayer, and then take the one area you are holding back and give it to God in some concrete act this week. A heart is unified the way a divided kingdom is, by surrendering one province at a time to the rightful King.

For worship. There was one man who was never in two minds. Jesus set his face to go to Jerusalem (Luke 9:51), and in the garden he prayed “Not my will, but yours, be done” (Luke 22:42). We are not saved by our singleness of heart; we are saved by his, and his Spirit works in us to make our divided hearts single.

verseByVerse.quote: Let the lowly brother boast in his exaltation, and the rich in his humiliation, because like a flower of the grass he will pass away. For the sun rises with its scorching heat and withers the grass; its flower falls, and its beauty perishes. So also will the rich man fade away in the midst of his pursuits.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The lowly brother. James turns to money, and he will keep coming back to it. Lowly means humble, of low status, and among these scattered believers it often meant genuinely poor. He is told to boast in his high position: not in his poverty, nor only in a reward to come, but in what he already is, a child of God and an heir of the kingdom (2:5). His social position is the least true thing about him.

The rich in his humiliation. The two halves mirror each other, and each says the opposite of what the world says. The rich believer is to boast in being brought low: in discovering that his money buys nothing where it counts, that he came to God with empty hands like everybody else, a sinner saved by grace on the same level as the poorest member of his church. That is a harder boast, and the only one available to him. God has always reversed the world’s rankings: “he has brought down the mighty from their thrones and exalted those of humble estate” (Luke 1:52).

Both boasts meet at the cross. Both boasts make sense because both believers are joined to a Saviour who went down before he went up. Christ emptied himself, took the form of a servant and became obedient to death on a cross; therefore God has highly exalted him (Philippians 2:7–9). The Lord of glory was brought lower than any refugee: born in a borrowed place, buried in a borrowed tomb, stripped even of his clothes. The lowly believer’s exaltation is his: God has raised us up with him and seated us with him in the heavenly places (Ephesians 2:6). The rich believer’s humiliation is his too: to kneel at the same cross with the same empty hands. In Christ every member of the church kneels on the same floor and is seated on the same throne.

Like a flower of the grass. The image is from Isaiah 40:6–8, which his readers knew by heart: all flesh is grass, the grass withers, the flower fades.

In the midst of his pursuits. The word means journeys, business trips. Not after them, when he can look back, but in the middle of them, with the plans half-made and the diary full: the man in the Lord’s parable who had just decided to build bigger barns and was told, “This night your soul is required of you” (Luke 12:16–21). Wealth does not protect from death. It only gives a man more to leave behind.

What it does not mean. It does not mean wealth is sinful: Abraham and Job were rich and loved God. Wealth is temporary and gives no standing before God.

Where Christians differ: is the rich man in verse 10 a believer? Some think brother carries over, so James is telling rich Christians to glory in their humbling. Others note that the rich in this letter are always outsiders and oppressors (2:6–7; 5:1–6), and read the line as bitter irony: let the rich man boast in the only thing coming to him, which is his destruction. Both readings are held by careful interpreters. The first fits the grammar a little better and gives a word to wealthy church members; the second fits the rest of the letter. Either way the lesson for us is the same: money is a flower, and anyone who builds his life on it is building on something that will be brown by evening.

Who counts as rich today? Most of us reading this. If you have food for tomorrow, a roof, a choice about what to wear, and some savings or a pension, then by any historical or global measure you are rich. It is easy to read James and think of billionaires. He would read it to us. That is not meant to produce guilt but freedom: to hold what you have loosely, to give generously (1 Timothy 6:17–19), and to find your boast not in what you own but in being a beggar who has been made an heir.

I am poor, and I am ashamed of it. What does this say to me? It says your poverty is real but it is not the truest thing about you. In God’s house there is no second class. You are a son or daughter of the King, and your inheritance cannot be repossessed (1 Peter 1:4). Hold your head up in church. And if you are in real need, it is not shameful to let your brothers and sisters help; the early church shared so that no one among them was needy (Acts 4:34), and that is still how a church is meant to work.

In everyday life. Read last month’s bank statement as a diary, because it is one: what does it say you love? Then do one thing that loosens money’s grip, gladly, because your riches are in Christ: give something away quietly, or cancel something you do not need.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed is the man who remains steadfast under trial, for when he has stood the test he will receive the crown of life, which God has promised to those who love him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blessed. The word of the Beatitudes (Matthew 5:3–12): happy, approved by God. Here is the outcome that makes it reasonable to count trials as joy (v. 2). “Remains steadfast” is the verb form of the steadfastness of verse 3.

When he has stood the test. The assayer’s word again, and this time as a verdict rather than a process. The metal has been through the fire and passed. The trial had a purpose, and the purpose was reached.

The crown of life. The crown is usually the victor’s wreath at the games rather than a royal diadem (2 Timothy 4:8; 1 Peter 5:4; Revelation 2:10). And the phrase almost certainly means the crown which is life: not a decoration worn on top of eternal life, but eternal life itself as the prize.

Promised to those who love him. Two clauses keep this from being a wage. It is a crown God has promised, so it rests on a promise, not on the quality of the endurance. And it is promised to those who love him, not to those who endure impressively. The person described is not a stoic with unusual reserves of grit; he loves God, and the steadfastness is what love looks like when it is put under weight.

The Lord’s own beatitude. James is repeating his brother: “the one who endures to the end will be saved” (Matthew 10:22), with the very verb used here. And the life that is the crown is not a prize handed out beside Christ, who is the resurrection and the life (John 11:25): to receive the crown of life is to receive him.

A verse facing two ways. It closes the passage on trials from outside, and its word for trial is the same one that means temptation, which is what James turns to next. The same hard circumstance that God uses to prove our faith, our own desire can use to draw us into sin, so we need to know which of the two is at work.

What if I did not endure well? I gave in, or grew bitter, or nearly walked away. Then hear the gospel before you hear anything else: the crown rests on God’s promise, not on your performance. Peter denied Christ three times in one night and was restored by Jesus beside a fire on the beach (John 21:15–19). Endurance in Scripture is not a perfect record but a faith that keeps getting up and coming back. If you are reading this and still want Christ, you have not fallen away; you have stumbled, and the God who began a good work in you will finish it. Confess what went wrong, receive his forgiveness, and take the next step.

Are there different crowns for different Christians? The New Testament speaks of crowns in several places: of life, of righteousness, of glory (2 Timothy 4:8; 1 Peter 5:4). These are best read not as separate prizes for an elite but as different ways of describing the one great gift every believer receives: eternal life with Christ, the righteousness he gives, the glory he shares. Scripture does teach that faithful service will be rewarded (1 Corinthians 3:12–15), but no believer will be outside the joy, and the elders in Revelation cast their crowns before the throne (Revelation 4:10). The crowns end up at his feet.

In everyday life. Someone in your church is under a long trial: an illness, a hard marriage, a disabled child, a slow grief. Endurance is often lonely. Send them a message today, or visit, and tell them you see what they are carrying.

For worship. Jesus was crowned with glory and honour because of the suffering of death (Hebrews 2:9). Soldiers twisted thorns into a wreath and pressed it on his head as a joke, and God made the joke the truth: the King of glory was crowned there, in our place, under our curse. He wore the crown of thorns so that we could wear the crown of life, and he will set it on every head that loved him, however bruised.

verseByVerse.quote: Let no one say when he is tempted, “I am being tempted by God,” for God cannot be tempted with evil, and he himself tempts no one. But each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire. Then desire when it has conceived gives birth to sin, and sin when it is fully grown brings forth death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Tempted by God. Now the same Greek word shifts in meaning from testing to tempting: an inner pull towards sin. Somebody was saying it, or James would not forbid it, and the excuse is perennial. He made me this way. He put the opportunity in front of me. The first man did it within minutes of the first sin: “The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me fruit of the tree, and I ate” (Genesis 3:12). Not simply “the woman”, but “the woman whom you gave”.

God cannot be tempted. The answer comes in two parts, and both are absolute. God is untemptable: there is nothing in him for evil to appeal to, no foothold, no answering appetite. He is utterly holy, light in whom is no darkness at all (1 John 1:5).

He himself tempts no one. Yet God does test: he tested Abraham (Genesis 22:1), and James has just spent eleven verses saying trials do good work. The difference is in the aim: a test is designed to prove and strengthen; a temptation is designed to destroy. One circumstance can be both at once, and the difference lies in who is using it for what. Joseph’s brothers meant it for evil; God meant it for good (Genesis 50:20).

Lured and enticed. Then James names the real source, and it is closer to home. Both verbs come from hunting and fishing: lured is to be drawn out of cover; enticed is from the word for bait. The picture is a fish drawn from under the rock by something that looks like food, with the hook hidden inside it. And James says whose desire it is: “his own”. The source is not the circumstance, and not even the devil, whom James does not mention here. The devil does tempt (Matthew 4:1–11), but he can only dangle the bait. The bait works because of what is already in the fish.

Desire gives birth to sin. The metaphor changes to conception and birth. Desire, welcomed and embraced by the will, conceives. It gives birth to sin, the act. Sin grows to full term, and what it delivers is death (Romans 6:23): a terrible genealogy.

Every stage looks manageable. A desire is not yet a sin, and can be entertained. A sin is small and can be handled. James lays the whole line out in one sentence so that you can see the end from the beginning, which is the one thing desire never lets you do. The bait never shows you the hook, and the first step never shows you the grave.

The one the bait could not catch. James’s analysis has one exception, and the Gospels show him in the desert. Jesus was truly tempted: hungry and alone, he was offered bread, safety and the kingdoms of the world (Matthew 4:1–11). But the hook found nothing to catch on. He felt the full pull of temptation, more than we ever do, because he never gave in and so never felt it slacken. There was no sinful desire in him for the bait to draw out, which is why he could say, “the ruler of this world is coming. He has no claim on me” (John 14:30). Where the first Adam, in a garden full of food, blamed “the woman whom you gave”, the last Adam, starving in a wilderness, answered every lie with “It is written”, and blamed no one. The genealogy of desire, sin and death was reversed in him: he took our death, and gives us his life.

Where Christians differ: if God is sovereign over all things, is he the author of sin? Some object that the Reformed view of God’s sovereignty makes God responsible for evil. This commentary’s view: God is sovereign over all things, including the sinful acts of human beings, which he permits and overrules for his good purposes (Genesis 50:20; Acts 2:23; 4:27–28). Yet he is never the author of sin, never tempts anyone, and never approves of evil (Westminster Confession 5.4; 1689 London Baptist Confession 5.4). Sin arises from the creature’s own desires. God’s sovereignty and human responsibility are both taught in Scripture and must both be held, even when we cannot fully explain how they fit together. The cross is the proof: the most wicked act in history was planned by God for the salvation of the world, and the men who did it were guilty of it.

Then why does the Lord’s Prayer say lead us not into temptation? God brings his people into trials, but never to make them sin. In that prayer (Matthew 6:13) we ask to be kept from trials that would overwhelm us, and to be delivered from the evil one when they come. It is the prayer of someone who knows his own weakness and does not trust himself, which is exactly the posture James wants.

Is being tempted itself a sin? No. Our Lord himself was tempted in every respect as we are, and never once sinned (Hebrews 4:15). Sin begins when the desire is welcomed and cherished, when it conceives (v. 15). A temptation resisted is a victory, not a failure. Many sensitive Christians are tormented by thoughts they hate. The thought that arrives uninvited is the bait being dangled; it becomes sin when you take it in, turn it over, and want it. The very fact that you hate it shows whose side you are on.

So what do I actually do in the moment of temptation? Name it honestly: this is my desire, not God’s plan. Look past the bait to the hook, and say to yourself where this leads. Then flee if you can (2 Timothy 2:22); Joseph left his cloak and ran. Pray, briefly and immediately, because he is able to help those who are being tempted (Hebrews 2:18). Fill the empty space with something good, and tell a trusted friend afterwards, since secrecy is the womb where desire conceives. And remember the promise: God is faithful, and he will not let you be tempted beyond your ability, but will provide the way of escape (1 Corinthians 10:13).

In everyday life. Trace the genealogy of your most frequent temptation. When does the desire usually begin: tiredness, loneliness, a particular screen, person or hour of the night? That is where the battle is won or lost, long before the act. And stop saying, even silently, that it is not really your fault. Taking the blame is the beginning of freedom, because the blame you own is the blame Christ has already carried, and those who walk by the Spirit will not gratify the desires of the flesh (Galatians 5:16).

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be deceived, my beloved brothers. Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no variation or shadow due to change. Of his own will he brought us forth by the word of truth, that we should be a kind of firstfruits of his creatures.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not be deceived, my beloved brothers. The lie about God, that he is behind your temptation, that he set you up, is not a harmless mistake. It is a deception, and James corrects it not by argument but by describing what God is actually like.

Every good gift. The traffic runs one way. Nothing bad comes down that road. If it is good, it came from there; if it came from there, it is good. In Greek the line has a poetic rhythm, almost a hexameter, and may be a saying James is quoting. The first phrase, “good gift”, stresses the act of giving; the second, “perfect gift”, is the thing given, complete. God gives well, and what he gives is whole.

The Father of lights. The maker of sun, moon and stars (Genesis 1:14–18; Psalm 136:7–9), a title chosen for the sake of what follows, because the one thing everybody knows about heavenly lights is that they change. Sun, moon and shadows shift all day long.

No shadow due to change. The shadow due to change is the shadow cast by turning, as it moves round a sundial or the moon passes through its phases. The Father who made the changing lights does not himself change (Malachi 3:6; Hebrews 13:8). There is no season in him, no eclipse, no angle from which he looks different. Theologians call this God’s immutability: he cannot change.

The light does not flicker. When you are in a trial, the temptation is not usually to doubt God’s existence. It is to suspect that he has gone cool: that he was favourable last year and is not now. James says the light does not flicker. Your circumstances turn like the sky; the one who loves you does not.

He brought us forth. Then the supreme instance of the good gift. Of his own will: God’s sovereign choice. Brought forth is a birth word, deliberately, because it answers verse 15, where sin, full-grown, brought forth death with the same verb. Two pregnancies, two deliveries, three verses apart: sin gives birth to death; God gives birth to life. This is regeneration, the new birth (John 1:13; 3:3–8; 1 Peter 1:3, 23).

By the word of truth. The word of truth is the gospel (Ephesians 1:13; Colossians 1:5). The new birth begins with God’s will, and he uses his word to do it (1 Peter 1:23). No one is born again without hearing of Christ, and no one who is born again can take the credit, because no one has ever caused his own birth. Before you wanted him, he willed you; before you could speak, he spoke his word of truth into your death, and you lived.

Firstfruits. The word (aparchē) is harvest language: the first sheaf brought in and offered to God, which is both a real portion and a pledge that the whole harvest belongs to him (Leviticus 23:10). These scattered believers are the opening instalment of a renewed creation; the whole groaning creation will follow (Romans 8:19–23).

Firstfruits of the risen firstfruits. The harvest began on a particular morning. Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep (1 Corinthians 15:20). The first sheaf of the new creation was the body that came out of the tomb, and the word of truth by which God brings us forth is the news that Christ died for our sins and was raised (1 Corinthians 15:3–4). The new birth is being joined to him, born again to a living hope through his resurrection (1 Peter 1:3), and every believer is a sheaf from the field whose first sheaf was Christ.

What it does not mean. Of his own will he brought us forth does not mean our response is unreal. We truly believe and truly repent. But our new birth originates in God’s sovereign will, not in our decision (John 1:13). The new birth (regeneration) comes before faith and produces it: you did not come alive by believing; you believed because God had already made you alive, as Lazarus walked out of the tomb only because the voice of Jesus had first given him life (John 11:43–44; Ephesians 2:4–5). Christians in the Arminian tradition, who hold that God’s grace enables every hearer to believe and that the new birth follows faith, read verses like this differently, and they too give God the glory for their salvation; this commentary holds the Reformed order because Scripture traces the new birth to God’s will before ours (John 1:13; Ephesians 2:4–5).

If God never changes, why does the Bible say he relented? When Scripture says God relented or changed his mind (Jonah 3:10), it is describing God’s dealings from our side: his settled character is to punish the unrepentant and spare the repentant, so when people turn, his response turns with them. His purposes and character do not change; that is exactly why his responses are so reliable. And it is why prayer is worth praying. We do not pray to a God who might be in a different mood today, but to one who has promised to hear and whose promises do not shift.

Does every good gift include good things unbelievers enjoy? Yes. Every sunrise, harvest, friendship, piece of music, act of healing and moment of laughter, whoever enjoys it, comes down from the Father of lights. Theologians call this common grace: “he makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good” (Matthew 5:45). The tragedy of the unbeliever is not that he receives no gifts but that he never thanks the Giver (Romans 1:21). The joy of the believer is to trace every good thing back up the road it came down.

In everyday life. If you are a believer, remember that you did not bring about your own new birth; that means you cannot undo it on a bad day either.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The word that gave new birth is to be received humbly and done, not only heard. James then puts that to three tests that open the rest of the letter: the tongue, care for the helpless, and a life unstained by the world.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Mirror

Hearing without doing is self-deception. The blessed man looks into the perfect law of liberty, stays there, and acts.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Orphans and widows were the people with no one to speak for them.

Now: Pure religion still means turning up for the helpless and keeping unstained from the world: both, not one.

verseByVerse.quote: Know this, my beloved brothers: let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger; for the anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Know this, my beloved brothers. Either “you know this” or “take note of this”; the Greek can be read both ways. Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, read “wherefore” here instead; the earliest have “know this”.

Not conversational tips. The setting of this verse is the word of truth (v. 18) and the implanted word (v. 21). James is saying how to receive Scripture, and then, because the same posture governs both, how to treat each other. The man who listens to God properly will begin to listen to people properly, and the man who interrupts God will interrupt everybody.

Quick to hear. Eager, leaning in, ready, the first instinct. It is the opposite of the man who already knows. Especially toward God’s word, but also toward others: hearing the whole sentence, the whole story, the thing behind the thing.

Slow to speak. This is not a call to silence; James preaches, and his letter is full of words. It is about order and speed (Proverbs 10:19; 17:27–28). A word that comes out too fast has not been weighed, and among pressured and frightened people the quick word was doing damage.

Slow to anger. He does not say “never angry”. “Slow” allows that some things ought to produce it, and insists that arriving there quickly is the fault. God himself is slow to anger (Exodus 34:6), and James is asking his readers to be like their Father.

The anger of man. Produce means work out, accomplish; the righteousness of God here is the righteous life God requires. That is a hard word for people angry about something genuine. Many of these readers were poor, some were being cheated by employers (5:4), and James thinks that scandalous. He does not say the anger is unjustified. He says it will not produce what it is aiming at.

One sequence. That also explains the order of the three commands. A man slow to hear and quick to speak will be quick to anger; they are one sequence, and it begins with how you listen. Most quarrels are lost at the first stage, when one person stopped hearing and started preparing his reply.

The ear that was opened every morning. The order James gives was once lived without a break. Isaiah’s Servant says that the Lord has given him the tongue of those who are taught, to sustain the weary with a word, and that morning by morning he awakens his ear to hear (Isaiah 50:4). And when he was reviled, the one with every right to anger was like a lamb led to the slaughter, and did not open his mouth (Isaiah 53:7; 1 Peter 2:23). Quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger: before it was a command to us, it was the life of the one who obeyed in our place.

What it does not mean. It does not forbid all anger: “be angry and do not sin” (Ephesians 4:26), and Jesus looked around at the Pharisees with anger, grieved at their hardness of heart (Mark 3:5). But human anger is usually mixed with pride and self-interest, and it must not be quick.

Does this mean I should stay quiet when I am being wronged or abused? No. Slow to anger is not a command to accept abuse or to keep quiet about wrongdoing. Scripture commands us to defend the weak and expose deeds of darkness (Psalm 82:3–4; Ephesians 5:11). If you or anyone else is being harmed, speak up, get help, and if a crime is involved, go to the authorities. What James forbids is the hot, quick, self-righteous anger that lashes out and makes things worse. Righteous action is often calm, deliberate and firm. Justice is better served by a clear head than by a burning one.

How do I become slow to anger when it rises so fast? Start with the first command: be quick to hear. Most anger is fed by assuming the worst. Before you answer, ask a question: what did you mean by that? Give yourself time: a walk, a night’s sleep, an unsent email. Ask what your anger is protecting: often it is pride or fear. Bring it to God before you bring it to the person (Psalm 4:4). And remember how slow God has been with you. Nothing cools anger like remembering how patient he is with us.

In everyday life. Online is where this rule matters most: read the post twice, wait an hour, and ask whether your reply will build anything.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore put away all filthiness and rampant wickedness and receive with meekness the implanted word, which is able to save your souls.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Put away all filthiness. The verb is the one used of taking off a garment (Colossians 3:8). Filthiness is moral dirt, and a related word was used in medical writing of earwax, which blocks hearing. Whether or not James intended the pun, the point stands: sin blocks our ears to God’s word. A man cannot be quick to hear with his ears stopped.

Rampant wickedness. Rampant means an overflow, an excess that spills; wickedness is malice. The picture is of something that has grown past its bounds and needs cutting back before anything else can grow: the excess of evil that remains even in believers.

Receive with meekness. Take off, and take in: you cannot do the second while wearing the first. Receive means welcome, as you would a guest. Meekness is not weakness but strength that has stopped fighting back, the opposite of the anger of verse 20. Applied to Scripture it means coming without a case to argue: not sitting in judgment on the text, not sifting it for what confirms you, but letting it have the last word.

The implanted word. Emphytos means innate or engrafted, planted in, rooted. So the word is not merely something they hear from outside; it has been planted in them at their new birth (v. 18), and their job is to let it grow rather than to fetch it.

Able to save your souls. Not able to inform or improve; it has power to save. Save your souls means the final salvation of the whole person (5:20; 1 Peter 1:9). James is often accused of teaching mere good behaviour. Yet he rests all the commands that follow on something God has planted, which does the saving.

Planted by a covenant sealed in blood. The word could be planted in these hearts only because of a table and a cross. The promise behind the implanted word, “I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts” (Jeremiah 31:33), is the new covenant, and on the night he was betrayed Jesus said, “This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood” (Luke 22:20). The implanted word is not self-help absorbed by effort but a gift his death bought and his Spirit sows.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers are not yet saved at all. They have been born again (v. 18). But salvation has past, present and future aspects: we have been saved from sin’s penalty, are being saved from its power, and will be saved from its presence. The word keeps working until the end.

What does meekness toward Scripture look like when I find a passage hard or I disagree with it? It means assuming that if there is a conflict between you and the Bible, you are the one who needs to move. Read the hard passage carefully, in context; ask what it actually says, not what you fear it says. Seek help from good teachers. Bring your questions to God honestly; the psalmists did. But do not edit Scripture to fit your preferences. Meekness is not pretending to have no questions. It is bringing them to the word as a pupil, not as a judge.

In everyday life. A sin you are holding onto will make every sermon sound like someone else’s problem. Before you read, pray, “Speak, LORD, for your servant hears”; then read until something cuts against you, and stay there.

verseByVerse.quote: But be doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving yourselves.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But be doers of the word. This is the thesis of the letter, and everything to chapter 5 applies it. And doer (poiētēs, from which comes poet, a maker) is a noun: it describes what a person is, not one thing he once did. Receiving the word (v. 21) must lead to doing it, and the doing grows out of a gift: the Father brought us forth by this same word of truth (v. 18), and the word that gave us life goes on working in those who obey it.

And not hearers only. James does not disparage hearing; he has just commanded it. The problem is the word only. Hearers are an audience, those who attend lectures. The man in view is not a man who refuses Scripture. He is a man who attends.

Deceiving yourselves. The term means to reason falsely, to talk yourself into a wrong conclusion. This is not hypocrisy, which deceives other people. It is a man doing the sum wrong about himself and believing the answer, which is why it is so dangerous: a hypocrite knows, and this man does not. He has heard the word, felt its force, agreed with it warmly, and counted his agreeing as though it were doing.

A peculiarly religious danger. And it grows with exposure. The more sermons a person hears, the more familiar the sensation of being moved becomes, and the easier it is to mistake for change. It can even become a quiet way of trusting ourselves: our seriousness about the Bible, our notes and our attendance start to feel like the thing that makes us right with God, when the word we hear keeps pointing us away from ourselves to Christ.

These words of mine. James is restating how his brother ended the Sermon on the Mount: everyone who hears these words of mine and does them will be like a wise man who built his house on the rock (Matthew 7:24–27). Doing them does not earn a place with him. It is building on him.

Does James contradict Paul here? No. Paul also says it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God (Romans 2:13), and he insists that faith works through love (Galatians 5:6). Both apostles teach that we are saved by grace through faith alone, and that the faith which saves is never alone; it always bears fruit (Ephesians 2:8–10). Paul is fighting people who want to add works to faith as the ground of salvation; James is fighting people who think faith can be real without works. They stand back to back, facing different enemies. James makes the same case at length in chapter 2, where Abraham and Rahab show that the faith which justifies is a living, working faith (2:14–26).

I have been a hearer for years. Where do I even start? Not with a programme but with one thing. Take the clearest thing God has said to you recently, the thing you already know you should do, and do it this week. Most of us are not short of information; we are carrying a backlog of obedience. Start at the front of the queue. And do not despair over the years: the God who planted the word is patient, and a hearer who begins to do is exactly what this verse is for.

For worship. There has been one perfect doer of the word. Jesus did not only hear his Father; “My food,” he said, “is to do the will of him who sent me and to accomplish his work” (John 4:34). Every word he heard, he did, all the way to the cross, and there was never a gap between his hearing and his doing, not even in Gethsemane. We never obey like that, but his unbroken obedience is counted as ours, the righteousness in which his people stand, and it is also the life his Spirit is reproducing in them, slowly, word by word. The Doer is making doers, and he will finish what he has begun.

verseByVerse.quote: For if anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he is like a man who looks intently at his natural face in a mirror. For he looks at himself and goes away and at once forgets what he was like.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A mirror. He does not glance: the verb means to look intently, to study. The hearer in this picture is not careless in the moment; he is engaged. His natural face is literally the face of his birth: what he was born with, and cannot alter by wishing.

At once forgets. The failure lies entirely in what comes next, and three verbs tell it. He looked, genuinely. He left. And by the time he was through the door it was gone, not gradually but at once.

What is a mirror for? Not admiration. You look in one to find out what needs attention: the smudge, the collar, the thing you cannot see without help. A mirror is there to show what is wrong, and its whole value lies in what you do in the ten seconds after you turn away. Scripture is like a mirror: it shows us what we really are. So the man in the illustration has performed the ritual of self-examination and skipped the point of it. He has confused looking with acting.

The face that shows us ours. The word does its sharpest work as a mirror when it shows us Christ. Peter had heard Jesus teach from his boat; then he saw the nets break, fell at Jesus’ knees and said, “Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord” (Luke 5:8). He had looked at Jesus, and seen himself. That is how Scripture exposes us: not chiefly by a list of faults but by setting the Holy One before us. And the mirror that exposes us is the same mirror in which, beholding the glory of the Lord, we are slowly made like him (2 Corinthians 3:18). And Jesus did not leave Peter on his knees: “Do not be afraid; from now on you will be catching men” (Luke 5:10). The look that exposes is meant to lead straight into following, which is exactly what the forgetful man never does.

How do I stop forgetting? Make the response before you leave the mirror. When a passage or a sermon shows you something, act on it while the image is fresh: confess the sin then and there, send the apology that day, write the one sentence of what you will do on a card you will see tomorrow. Tell someone, because things spoken aloud are harder to forget. Reread the passage the next morning. Forgetting is not usually a failure of memory but a failure to act quickly; what we act on, we remember.

Does the mirror only show my faults? No, and this matters for tender consciences. The same Scripture that shows you your sin shows you your Saviour, and who you are in him: forgiven, adopted, loved. A person who only ever sees condemnation in the mirror is not reading the whole of it. Look until you see both: what needs washing, and the one who washes.

verseByVerse.quote: But the one who looks into the perfect law, the law of liberty, and perseveres, being no hearer who forgets but a doer who acts, he will be blessed in his doing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The perfect law. The verb for “looks” is stronger than the one in verse 23: to stoop down and peer in, used of Peter, John and Mary Magdalene bending to look into the empty tomb (Luke 24:12; John 20:5, 11). Not a glance in passing but a posture: bending over the thing to see it properly. Peter uses the same word of angels longing to look into the salvation the prophets foretold (1 Peter 1:12). Angels stoop to look into this salvation; we are allowed to stoop and look, and to stay. And the perfect law (complete, mature) is God’s word, including the moral law as fulfilled and interpreted by Christ, the royal law of love (2:8).

The law of liberty. The phrase sounds like a contradiction and is not. James does not mean law as a way of earning God’s favour; he has just said the implanted word saves. He means God’s revealed will as it now stands in Christ, and it liberates because it is no longer a standard you must reach in order to be accepted. It is written on the heart by the Spirit (Jeremiah 31:33) and obeyed from love, not compulsion: true freedom is the freedom to do what is right, released from slavery to sin (Romans 8:2). You keep it as a freed man, not as a slave earning his way out. And the law of liberty also judges (2:12).

And perseveres. The word means to remain beside, to stay bent over it, the exact opposite of goes away. The difference between the two men is not the quality of the looking. It is that one of them stayed.

If you abide in my word. Jesus joined staying and freedom first. “If you abide in my word,” he told those who had believed him, “you are truly my disciples, and you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free”; and “if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed” (John 8:31–32, 36). The law’s freedom is not in the commandments by themselves but in the Son who kept them for us and stands behind every one of them as a friend, not an accuser. The man who stays bent over the word is staying with Christ, and that is where freedom lives.

A doer who acts. Literally “a doer of work”: for James, real obedience always leaves something done.

Blessed in his doing. As in verse 12. Not blessed for it, as though the doing purchased a reward, but blessed in it: the blessing is inside the obedience (John 13:17; Psalm 1:1–3). The man who does what he has seen finds that the doing is itself the good thing, which the man walking away from the mirror never discovers.

Which law is this? Are Christians under the Ten Commandments? Christians are not under the law as a covenant of works, a way of earning acceptance or facing condemnation; Christ has fulfilled it and borne its curse for us (Galatians 3:13). But the moral law, summed up in the Ten Commandments and in love for God and neighbour, remains the rule of life for believers, showing us God’s will and our duty (Westminster Confession 19.6; 1689 London Baptist Confession 19.6). That is what James means: not the ceremonial laws of temple and sacrifice, which Christ fulfilled, but God’s holy will as Jesus taught it. Kept in love, it is not a cage but a road.

Blessed in doing. Does obedience always feel good? Not always in the moment. Forgiving someone who hurt you, telling the truth when it costs, giving when money is tight: these can feel like loss. The blessing James means is deeper than a pleasant feeling. It is the quiet rightness of walking with God, a clear conscience, fruit that grows over time, and the experience of God’s presence and help in the very act. Often the blessing is recognised only looking back. But no one who has obeyed God has ever, in the end, regretted it.

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone thinks he is religious and does not bridle his tongue but deceives his heart, this person’s religion is worthless. Religion that is pure and undefiled before God the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their affliction, and to keep oneself unstained from the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If anyone thinks he is religious. Thinks means supposes, seems to himself. Religious refers to religion’s outward exercise: the observances, worship and visible practice. He attends, prays, fasts, and considers himself spiritual. James does not sneer at it. He asks what it is worth, and gives a startling answer, first negative (v. 26) and then positive (v. 27).

In the flow. Verses 26–27 put “be doers of the word” (v. 22) to three tests, and each opens a later part of the letter: the tongue (ch. 3), care for those with nothing to give (2:1–17), and friendship with the world (4:4).

Does not bridle his tongue. The bridle is the image James will develop at 3:2–3. Gossip, slander, harshness and lies contradict every religious claim. And of all the failures he could have chosen as the disqualifier, he chose speech, a sin most congregations tolerate entirely.

Worthless. Self-deception again (v. 22). Worthless means empty, futile, and it is applied not to an unbeliever but to a churchgoer with a loose mouth.

Pure and undefiled. Then the positive. Pure and undefiled are terms of ritual purity, and James fills them with practical love and moral holiness, as the prophets had done: “Wash yourselves; make yourselves clean,” Isaiah cried, and “plead the widow’s cause” (Isaiah 1:16–17). And “before God the Father” means what God, not people, counts as genuine. The only audience that matters is God.

Orphans and widows. Orphans and widows were the standard biblical shorthand for those with little legal protection and no income; in that society a woman without husband or sons often had no one to go to court for her. God is their defender: “Father of the fatherless and protector of widows is God in his holy habitation” (Psalm 68:5; Deuteronomy 10:18). The verb is visit, to look after, see to their needs; it is related to the word for overseer. It does not mean sending money from a distance. It means turning up.

God has visited his people. The verb has a history. When Jesus stopped a funeral at the gate of Nain, had compassion on a widow burying her only son, and gave the young man back to his mother, the crowd cried, “God has visited his people!” (Luke 7:11–16). True religion visits widows because the God of true religion did, in the person of his Son, and did not send help from a distance. Our visiting is his visitation still going on through his people.

Unstained from the world. Two things, and they are usually pulled apart by people who prefer one. Care for the defenceless, and personal holiness. James joins them with an “and” and gives no permission to choose. Unstained means spotless. The world here is human society organised in rebellion against God, with its values, desires and pressures (4:4; 1 John 2:15–17).

How does this apply today? In caring for orphans through adoption and fostering, for single mothers, for the lonely elderly and for widows in the church, in personal kindness and in the church’s organised care. And to keep oneself unstained from the world means to refuse the values of a world opposed to God (4:4; 1 John 2:15–17): its greed, its pride, its view of sex, its contempt for the weak.

What it does not mean. It does not mean caring for the needy is the whole of religion, or that worship and doctrine do not matter. James assumes faith in Christ (2:1), and he says that those who believe that God is one “do well” (2:19). He is showing what genuine faith looks like in practice, as opposed to empty ritual. He is naming the test. If you want to know whether the word has been implanted, do not look at the intensity of the hearing. Look at whether anyone with nothing to offer you has seen you lately.

Is caring for the needy the same as preaching the gospel? No. The gospel is the announcement of what Christ has done for sinners, and nothing replaces telling people about him (Romans 10:14). But mercy is the fruit and the adornment of the gospel, and a church that preaches grace and ignores the widow down the street is contradicting its own message. Begin with the household of faith (Galatians 6:10), the widows and the struggling in your own church, and then go out to the neighbour. Word and deed belong together, as they did in Jesus’ ministry.

Does unstained from the world mean I should withdraw from society? No. Jesus prayed not that his people be taken out of the world but kept from the evil one (John 17:15). The visiting of orphans and widows takes you right into the world’s mess. Being unstained means not absorbing its values while you serve in it: going into the hospital, the care home, the hard estate, without adopting the greed, cynicism and lust that the world takes for granted. As Jesus ate with tax collectors and sinners and was never stained by their sin (Hebrews 7:26), the Christian goes in close and stays clean, by God’s grace.

In everyday life. Who near you has no one to go to court for them, the widow, the foster child, the lonely old man, and when did you last turn up at their door?

For worship. We were orphans, and the Father adopted us. The Son came down into the world’s filth, touched lepers and ate with sinners without being stained, then took our stains onto himself on the cross, so that we could be presented holy and blameless and above reproach (Colossians 1:22). Pure and undefiled religion is the family likeness of a Father who has visited us.
