2.title: No Partiality: Faith That Sees Every Person
2.overview:
Chapter 2 has two linked parts. Verses 1–13 deal with favouritism in the church: the rich visitor gets a good seat and the poor man the floor. Verses 14–26 ask what real faith is. The poor visitor joins the two: a faith that shows him no love is dead faith.

James is not opposing Paul. He is opposing the idea that agreeing with true doctrine is saving faith; the demons agree with it. Living faith in Christ shows itself in works, as Abraham’s and Rahab’s did. Those works are the fruit of faith, not the ground of our standing with God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — The Gold Ring and the Royal Law
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Faith in the Lord Jesus cannot go with favouritism. James pictures a man with a gold ring given a good seat while a poor man is told to stand or sit on the floor. God has chosen the poor to be rich in faith. Favouritism breaks the royal law of love, so speak and act as those who will be judged by the law of liberty.
verseByVerse.theology:
One Lawgiver

Partiality contradicts faith in the Lord of glory and breaks the royal law. Whoever fails at one point is guilty before the one who gave the whole law. Mercy triumphs over judgment.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The congregation seated the man with the gold ring well and the poor man on the floor.

Now: The sin includes ranking people inside a welcome, not only shutting them out.

verseByVerse.quote: My brothers, show no partiality as you hold the faith in our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. James 2 shows in two movements that real faith works through love: it cannot fawn on the rich and shame the poor, for mercy triumphs over judgment (vv. 1–13), and it cannot stay mere talk, as Abraham and Rahab show (vv. 14–26). James is not contradicting Paul: both teach that saving faith is a living faith that produces works.

My brothers, show no partiality. The Greek word is built on a Hebrew idiom, to receive or lift the face, and in use it means partiality: judging by appearance, letting the look of a person decide how you treat them. Its background is the courtroom. The law forbade a judge to be partial to the poor or defer to the great (Leviticus 19:15), and grounded that in God himself, who is not partial and takes no bribe (Deuteronomy 10:17). James is about to describe a congregation behaving like a corrupt court.

As you hold the faith in our Lord Jesus Christ. Partiality is set directly against holding the faith: the man accused of preaching works opens his great chapter on works with faith in Jesus. And favouritism is not presented as bad manners. It is incompatible with the content of what they believe, and the rest of the verse says why.

The Lord of glory. The Greek is stark, literally “our Lord Jesus Christ, of the glory”, and it is the highest thing James says about his brother anywhere in the letter. It may even be a title, Jesus the Glory: God’s glory come to dwell among his people, as the cloud of glory once filled the tabernacle (Exodus 40:34; John 1:14). And glory belongs to God alone: “I am the LORD; that is my name; my glory I give to no other” (Isaiah 42:8). Whichever way the phrase is read, to give Jesus that glory is to call him God.

The placing is the argument. Set beside that glory, the difference between a gold ring and a poor man’s rags is nothing at all. When the sun is up, nobody compares candles. A congregation that seats people by their clothes has forgotten who is in the room.

The man who grew up with him. The man who says “the Lord of glory” grew up beside him in Nazareth, where there was no glory to see, and for a time did not believe in him at all (John 7:5). If anyone had learned that appearances mislead, it was James. He had sat at the same table as the Lord of glory for thirty years and seen a carpenter.

What it does not mean. It does not forbid all distinctions, such as honouring elders or respecting authorities (Romans 13:7). It forbids treating people differently because of wealth, status, race or appearance, especially in the church.

What does partiality look like in a church today? It rarely involves seats now, but it is the same sin. It is the visitor with a profession and a nice car who is invited to lunch, while the one with a carrier bag gets a handshake. It is noticing the gifted and the articulate for leadership and passing over the faithful and quiet. It is giving celebrities and large donors a platform their character has not earned. It is racial and cultural preference, the sense that some people are more our sort. And it can run the other way too: despising the wealthy or the educated is also judging by the face. The question to ask is plain: am I treating this person according to what Christ has made him, or according to what he can do for me?

Is it wrong to have closer friends at church? No. Jesus himself had Peter, James and John, and John was the disciple whom Jesus loved. Friendship is a gift. The sin James names is not having friends but ranking people’s worth: honouring some and humiliating others because of status. Enjoy your friends, and make sure the circle has an open side, so that the newcomer, the awkward and the poor are welcomed in as brothers and sisters, not tolerated at the edge.

For worship. The Lord of glory did not receive faces. He touched the leper, let a sinful woman weep on his feet, and called a despised little man down from a tree to host him. And when he chose his people, he did not choose by our clothes. He clothed us in his own righteousness, so that the poorest beggar who trusts him stands in garments brighter than any gold ring. Glory belongs to him alone, and he spends it on the lowly.

verseByVerse.quote: For if a man wearing a gold ring and fine clothing comes into your assembly, and a poor man in shabby clothing also comes in, and if you pay attention to the one who wears the fine clothing and say, “You sit here in a good place,” while you say to the poor man, “You stand over there,” or, “Sit down at my feet,” have you not then made distinctions among yourselves and become judges with evil thoughts?
verseByVerse.commentary:
For if a man wearing a gold ring and fine clothing. He puts a scene in front of them, and it is staged with a novelist’s eye. Two men arrive. The first is gold-fingered: perhaps wearing many rings, or the gold ring that in Roman society was not merely jewellery but a mark of rank. His clothing is literally shining, bright, splendid. He has dressed to be noticed and ranked.

Comes into your assembly. The word is synagogue. It is the only place in the New Testament where a Christian meeting is called a synagogue. It may refer to a worship service, or perhaps to a church court gathered to settle disputes between members (1 Corinthians 6:1–6), which would make the courtroom language even sharper.

And a poor man in shabby clothing also comes in. The word means filthy, the same root as the filthiness of 1:21. Not modest, not plain. Dirty, because he has nothing else and nowhere to wash it.

And if you pay attention to the one who wears the fine clothing. The verb means to look upon with favour, to gaze at admiringly. Every eye goes to the shining coat, and every face lights up.

You sit here in a good place. Then the treatment, and James gives it in direct speech so that they hear themselves saying it. To the first: here, comfortably, in a place of honour. To the second, two options, both an insult: stand at the back, or sit on the floor, literally under my footstool, down where a servant or a dog would be. A deliberate humiliation.

A genuine welcome. Nobody is thrown out. The poor man is let in and given a place. That is exactly what makes the scene so recognisable: the sin is not exclusion but ranking, and it operates entirely within a genuine welcome. Nobody in that room would have said they were against the poor. They gave him a place. They just made sure he knew which one. And underneath the seating lies a hunger of the heart: we honour the people whose approval we want, and we want it so badly because we have not yet rested in the approval of God, who has already welcomed us in Christ.

Have you not then made distinctions among yourselves. The verb means discriminated, been divided, and it is the same root as the doubting of 1:6. A church that sorts people has divided itself, and it is the double-mindedness of chapter 1 coming out in the seating.

And become judges with evil thoughts? That returns to the courtroom of verse 1. Literally judges whose reasonings are wicked. They have not merely been rude. They have made themselves a court, tried both men on the evidence of their clothing, and delivered verdicts, which is precisely the thing the law forbids a judge to do. They have set themselves up as judges of people’s worth, and their standards are corrupt.

But what if a wealthy visitor could really help the church? That is exactly the thought James is exposing, and it is why the sin is so tempting: it can be dressed up as good stewardship. The church does not need anyone’s money as much as it needs to be faithful. God provides for his work, and he has never needed a gold ring to do it. Welcome the wealthy visitor warmly, as warmly as anyone else, and no more. If he comes to Christ, he will learn to give gladly. If he is courted for his money, he learns that the church is like every other club, and the poor man learns it too.

What about someone who is dirty, smells, or is disruptive? Love does not pretend; it welcomes. Greet them, sit with them, offer a drink and something to eat, and treat them as you would want to be treated. If someone is genuinely disruptive or unsafe, elders and stewards should deal with it calmly and kindly, because protecting the congregation, especially children, is also love. But the default must be honour. The man in shabby clothes may be the one Christ sends to see how we treat him (Matthew 25:40).

In everyday life. Walk through your Sunday as a stranger with no money and no Christian vocabulary: where would you sit, who would speak to you, would anyone ask your name? Then be the one who does. Sit next to the person nobody sits next to, learn their name, and find out one thing about their week.

For worship. Christ took the footstool. He who has heaven as his throne and earth as his footstool (Isaiah 66:1) came down and was born where animals ate, and at the end he was stripped of his clothes, and soldiers threw dice for them. He stood in the place of the poor man in filthy clothes, so that we who were clothed in filthy rags before God could hear him say: take away his filthy garments, and clothe him with pure vestments (Zechariah 3:4). And then he says to the beggar he has dressed: “You sit here in a good place.” Sit with me on my throne (Revelation 3:21).

verseByVerse.quote: Listen, my beloved brothers, has not God chosen those who are poor in the world to be rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom, which he has promised to those who love him? But you have dishonored the poor man. Are not the rich the ones who oppress you, and the ones who drag you into court? Are they not the ones who blaspheme the honorable name by which you were called?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Has not God chosen those who are poor in the world. The first argument is from what God himself has done. Chosen is the language of election, God’s sovereign choice in salvation. Poor in the world means poor by worldly standards. This is not a claim that poverty qualifies anyone, or that every poor person is saved. It is how God has in fact worked: the early church was largely poor, and not many were wise or powerful or of noble birth (1 Corinthians 1:26). The force of it: God has been choosing exactly the people this congregation is seating on the floor.

To be rich in faith. Here is the reversal: poor in the world, rich in faith. Rich and poor are still there, but they have changed places. True riches are spiritual, and the man with the filthy coat may be the wealthiest person in the room.

And heirs of the kingdom, which he has promised to those who love him? Heirs of God’s reign, now and fully in the age to come (Matthew 5:3; 25:34). Those who love him is the phrase of 1:12, a description of true believers. The poor believer is a future king. The congregation is making a prince sit on the floor.

Chosen in his Chosen One. God’s choice of the poor is not a social policy; it is the shape of the gospel, because his Chosen One came poor. The Son of Man had nowhere to lay his head (Matthew 8:20), and the Father said of him, “This is my Son, my Chosen One” (Luke 9:35). That is why the kingdom belongs to the poor in spirit (Matthew 5:3): it is the kingdom of a King who emptied his hands first. God’s choice runs downward, and that is the glory of it. He chose a slave nation, a shepherd boy, a peasant girl in Nazareth, fishermen in Galilee; and he chose us when we had nothing to offer him but our sin. A congregation that despises the poor man is despising the likeness of its own Lord.

But you have dishonored the poor man. That is the charge, and the word is strong: to shame, to insult, to treat as worthless the very person God has honoured.

Are not the rich the ones who oppress you. The second and third arguments are brutally practical. Oppress means exercise power over, exploit, tyrannise. Wealthy landowners and creditors often exploited the poor, and these are not hypothetical rich men; chapter 5 will describe employers withholding wages from the men who mowed their fields (5:1–6).

And the ones who drag you into court? The verb means to haul by force, as Paul and Silas were dragged into the marketplace before the rulers (Acts 16:19). Perhaps over debts, perhaps because of their faith.

Are they not the ones who blaspheme the honorable name by which you were called? Blaspheme means slander, revile, speak evil of. The honourable name, literally the good, the beautiful name, is the name of Christ himself. By which you were called is literally the name which was called over you: an Old Testament phrase for ownership, used of Israel as the people called by God’s name, and probably pointing to baptism, when Christ’s name was pronounced over the believer, marking them as his (Acts 2:38). So the wealthy visitor being ushered to the good seat belongs to the class that exploits this congregation, takes it to court, and insults its Lord. Why fawn over people who mock your Lord?

The irrationality of flattery. James is not saying rich people are beyond salvation, and he is not telling them to favour the poor and snub the rich; verse 1 forbids that as much as the other. He is showing how senseless the flattery is. They are fawning on people who despise them, and they are doing it because of a ring.

Does God love the poor more than the rich? God shows no partiality (v. 1), and he does not choose anyone because of their bank balance, any more than because of their goodness. Election is of grace alone (Romans 11:5–6). But God has a special care for the poor and the oppressed, and he often chooses the weak to shame the strong, so that no one may boast (1 Corinthians 1:27–29). The rich face a particular danger: it is hard for them to feel their need (Matthew 19:23–26). The poor have often found it easier to come with empty hands, because their hands were already empty.

What does it mean that Christ’s name was called over me? It means you belong to him. In the Old Testament, to have God’s name called over a people, a city or the temple meant that God owned it and would defend it (Deuteronomy 28:10; Jeremiah 14:9). In the church this is marked in baptism, when a believer who has confessed Christ is baptised into the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit (Matthew 28:19). Whatever your church tradition, the point is the same: you carry his name. So treat others, and let yourself be treated, as people whose worth is set by the one whose name they wear.

In everyday life. Think of someone in your church who is poor in the world. God sees them as rich in faith and an heir of the kingdom, so go and learn from them: ask them how God has kept them.

verseByVerse.quote: If you really fulfill the royal law according to the Scripture, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself,” you are doing well. But if you show partiality, you are committing sin and are convicted by the law as transgressors.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If you really fulfill the royal law according to the Scripture. James anticipates the defence: “We were being hospitable; we were loving our neighbour.” “Really” means “if in fact”; “fulfil” means carry out. “Royal” probably means the King’s law: the supreme law that rules the others, given by the King and belonging to the kingdom just mentioned (v. 5).

You shall love your neighbor as yourself. He grants the principle, quoting Leviticus 19:18, and agrees that this is the standard. Love of neighbour sums up the second table of the law, the commandments that govern how we treat other people (Romans 13:8–10). And look where James found it: Leviticus 19:18 sits three verses after Leviticus 19:15, the very prohibition of partiality in judgment. He is quoting both halves of one paragraph, and his readers, who knew their Scriptures, would hear it.

But if you show partiality, you are committing sin. Then the trap closes. Loving your neighbour as yourself has no room for ranking: whichever man you seated well, you did not treat the other as yourself. And it is not a social failure. It is sin.

And are convicted by the law as transgressors. Back to the courtroom a third time, and now the seating committee is in the dock. They set themselves up as judges (v. 4); now the law puts them on trial. Convicted means exposed, proved guilty. And transgressor is a specific word: not a general sinner but one who has stepped over a line that was drawn and marked. The same law they claim to keep convicts them.

The King’s law and the King’s love. The law is royal because it belongs to a King. Jesus set Leviticus 19:18 beside the command to love God as the two on which all the Law and the Prophets depend (Matthew 22:37–40), and at the Last Supper he gave it a new measure: “just as I have loved you, you also are to love one another” (John 13:34). The standard is no longer only “as yourself”, but as he loved, by washing feet and laying down his life. Like the Samaritan in his own parable, he crossed the road to us when we lay half dead, poured in oil and wine, carried us on his own beast and paid for our care. The seating committee is being judged by the law of a King who knelt.

Does love your neighbour as yourself mean I must learn to love myself first? No. The command assumes that we already love ourselves, in the sense that we naturally care for our own needs, feed ourselves, protect ourselves, and want good things for ourselves (Ephesians 5:29). It does not command self-esteem; it commands that the same care be turned outward. Many people who feel they hate themselves are in fact very focused on themselves. The cure is not more attention to self but the love of God, which frees us to forget ourselves and attend to others.

Who counts as my neighbour? Jesus answered that question with the parable of the Good Samaritan (Luke 10:25–37). Your neighbour is whoever God puts in your path who needs your help, including the person of another race, class or religion, including the one you would naturally avoid. The lawyer wanted to limit the list. Jesus turned the question around: not who is my neighbour, but who proved to be a neighbour. In James’s scene the neighbour is the man in the filthy coat.

verseByVerse.quote: For whoever keeps the whole law but fails in one point has become guilty of all of it. For he who said, “Do not commit adultery,” also said, “Do not murder.” If you do not commit adultery but do murder, you have become a transgressor of the law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For whoever keeps the whole law but fails in one point. That sounds disproportionate, and everything depends on seeing why it is not. Fails means stumbles, trips. Even a single failure.

Has become guilty of all of it. Guilty means liable, answerable. The law is a unity, like a single sheet of glass: crack it anywhere and the whole is broken. A pane with a single hole in it is a broken window, not a mostly intact one.

For he who said, Do not commit adultery, also said, Do not murder. The reasoning is about the lawgiver rather than the law. One voice stands behind every command (Exodus 20:13–14; Deuteronomy 5:17–18), so the law is not a list from which you might keep most and fail a few. It is a single expression of one person’s will. Break any of it and you have not damaged one item on a list; you have set yourself against the one who spoke.

If you do not commit adultery but do murder, you have become a transgressor of the law. And the pairing of the examples is deliberate and pointed. Adultery and murder were probably the sins the congregation would have condemned most readily: the obvious, unarguable ones. James sets them beside seating the poor man on the floor and says: same court, same lawgiver, same verdict.

The grading of sins. That is what the argument is for. It takes away our private ranking of sins by how disreputable they look, in which our own (the impatience, the snobbery, the gossip, the little dishonesties) sit comfortably near the bottom. Partiality feels like a lapse of etiquette. James has just put it in a sentence with murder. That is humbling, and it is also freeing: the person whose sins are louder than yours is standing at the same cross as you, and the same blood covers you both.

What it does not mean. It does not mean all sins are equally serious in every respect. Scripture recognises degrees of sin and punishment (John 19:11; Luke 12:47–48), and plainly weighs consequences differently. The point is narrower and sharper: every sin puts you in the same relation to the same God, and no amount of law-keeping makes up for the part broken.

Then what hope does anyone have? None in the law, and that is exactly what the law is meant to teach. If one failure makes us guilty of all, then a lifetime of mostly keeping the rules cannot save anyone. Our only hope is a substitute who kept every point, and then bore the penalty for every point we broke. That is Christ: he was born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law (Galatians 4:4–5), and he became a curse for us (Galatians 3:13). James is not preaching despair. He is closing every other door so that we go through the only open one.

If I am already guilty of all, does it matter if I sin a little more? It matters enormously. Every sin offends the God who loves you, damages you and others, and grieves the Spirit (Ephesians 4:30). The point of this verse is not that sins do not matter, but that every sin matters more than we think. A forgiven believer does not reason: since I am covered, I may as well. He reasons: since he paid so much, how can I go on in what he died for (Romans 6:1–2)?

For worship. One voice spoke every command, and the same voice has spoken again. The Lawgiver who said “Do not commit adultery” and “Do not murder” came under his own law, kept every point of it, and was counted guilty of all of it in the place of his people. We never keep it whole, not even on our best days; the window we smashed was paid for with his blood, and now his obedience, whole and unbroken, is counted as ours. The glass is not patched; it is replaced with his. And the voice that thundered from Sinai said from the cross, “Father, forgive them” (Luke 23:34), and, “It is finished” (John 19:30).

verseByVerse.quote: So speak and so act as those who are to be judged under the law of liberty. For judgment is without mercy to one who has shown no mercy. Mercy triumphs over judgment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So speak and so act. Both verbs are present tense: keep on doing so. And the order matters in a letter this concerned with speech; the seating in verse 3 was done with words.

As those who are to be judged under the law of liberty. The phrase is from 1:25: God’s will as it stands in Christ, the law of love written on the heart, kept by people already accepted. But James does not use it to remove judgment. The freed man is still to be judged, and is expected to live accordingly.

For judgment is without mercy to one who has shown no mercy. Then verse 13, in two halves that must be held together. It restates the Lord’s own teaching: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall receive mercy” (Matthew 5:7), and the parable of the unforgiving servant (Matthew 18:21–35). And it must be read the right way round. A merciless person is not disqualified for failing to earn mercy. He is exposed: mercy received always produces mercy given, so a life with none flowing out is evidence that none has come in.

Mercy triumphs over judgment. The verb means to boast against, to exult over a defeated opponent. God’s mercy, received and shown, wins over judgment, and for those who have received mercy in Christ and show it to others, the judgment holds no terror. Judgment is real, and mercy is stronger, and the congregation seating men by their clothing is being asked which of the two it has been imitating.

Where mercy and judgment met. How can mercy triumph over judgment without justice being thrown away? Only at the cross. There God did not set aside his judgment against sin; he poured it out in full on his Son, our substitute, “so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:26). Mercy did not win by ignoring judgment. It won by bearing it. And on the last day the judgment seat will be occupied by the one who bore judgment for his people: those who stand before him will meet the Lamb who was slain, not a stranger weighing their record.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we earn God’s mercy by showing mercy. We show mercy because we have received it: “be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you” (Ephesians 4:32). But a merciless life is evidence of an unrenewed heart.

Will Christians really be judged? Yes, but not for condemnation. There is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). Every believer will stand before the judgment seat of Christ, where our lives are opened and what was done in his name is acknowledged and rewarded (2 Corinthians 5:10; 1 Corinthians 3:12–15). It is a Father’s assessment of his children, not a court deciding their fate. The thought should make us serious about our words and deeds, and it should never make a believer fear that Christ will cast him out.

I find it very hard to forgive someone who hurt me. Does that mean I have not received mercy? Not necessarily. Forgiveness of deep wounds is often a long process, and the struggle itself shows that you want to obey. The merciless person James describes does not struggle; he refuses and feels justified. Bring your hurt to God honestly, as the psalmists did, and ask him for the grace to forgive. Remember how much you have been forgiven. Forgiving means giving up your right to revenge and leaving judgment to God (Romans 12:19). It does not mean pretending it did not happen, or trusting the person again immediately.

Does showing mercy mean there should be no consequences? No. Mercy is not the same as excusing evil. If someone is abusing you, seek safety at once; forgiving him does not mean staying in danger, keeping silent, or protecting him from the law. The authorities exist to punish wrongdoing (Romans 13:4), and churches must report abuse and protect the vulnerable. Mercy refuses personal revenge and longs for the offender’s repentance; justice still holds him accountable. A church that covers up abuse in the name of mercy is not showing mercy to anyone, least of all the victim.

In everyday life. Listen to your own speech this week, since James says “so speak”. When you talk about the colleague who failed you, or the brother whose sin embarrassed the church, does it sound like someone who has been forgiven much? God in Christ has forgiven you; let that mercy reach your tongue first.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: What good is it to say you have faith if you have no works? Can that faith save? Kind words to a hungry brother, with no food given, are as dead as such faith. Abraham’s faith was shown and completed when he offered Isaac, and Rahab’s when she hid the spies. As the body without the spirit is dead, so is faith without works.
verseByVerse.theology:
Faith That Works

James asks whether a faith that is only said can save. Abraham was counted righteous by faith, and his obedience showed that faith was alive. Works do not earn justification; they are the fruit of the living faith that receives it.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The demons believe that God is one, and they shudder.

Now: Warm words to a hungry brother with nothing given are the picture of dead faith.

verseByVerse.quote: What good is it, my brothers, if someone says he has faith but does not have works? Can that faith save him?
verseByVerse.commentary:
What good is it, my brothers. Two small words in this verse settle a great deal. What good means what profit, what use, and it is the theme of the whole passage: useful faith versus useless faith.

If someone says he has faith but does not have works? The first key word is says. James is not describing a man who has faith. He is describing a man who claims it, and the whole question is whether the claim is true: a profession with no evidence. And works here are the deeds of love and obedience that living faith produces, like clothing and feeding a poor brother (vv. 15–16). They are not works of the law, moral or ceremonial, offered to God as grounds for acceptance; those, Paul says, can never justify anyone (Romans 3:20; 4:4–5).

Can that faith save him? The second key word is “that”. The Greek has “the faith” (hē pistis): can the faith just described, that kind of faith, save him? James is not asking whether faith saves. He is asking whether this thing does, and the form of the question in Greek expects the answer no. A faith that consists only of words, with no works, cannot save.

Where Christians differ: does James contradict Paul? Paul says we are justified by faith, not works (Romans 3:28; Galatians 2:16); James says a person is justified by works and not by faith alone (v. 24). Some have thought they contradict each other; Luther once called James an epistle of straw for this reason, though he kept it in his Bible and dropped the phrase from later editions of his preface. Roman Catholic teaching uses James to argue that justification includes good works. This commentary’s view: they do not contradict. They are answering different errors and using key words in different senses. Paul opposes legalism: those who think they can earn God’s acceptance by works of the law. James opposes empty profession: those who think a faith with no fruit can save. For Paul, justify means God’s declaration that a sinner is righteous, received through faith alone. For James, justify here means to show or prove righteous, as Abraham’s faith was vindicated by his deeds. For Paul, works means works of the law done to earn merit; for James, works of love that flow from faith. For Paul, faith means genuine trust in Christ; for James, in verse 14, faith means a mere claim to believe. Both agree that the faith which justifies always produces works (Galatians 5:6; Ephesians 2:8–10).

Back to back. Paul and James stand back to back, defending the same gospel on two sides: Paul against those trying to add works to Christ, James against those who have subtracted works entirely and are comfortable. James never contrasts faith with works; he contrasts living faith with dead faith. Works are the vital signs of living faith.

What faith holds. Behind James’s question lies a truth both apostles assume: faith does not save by being impressive, but by what it takes hold of. Faith is an empty hand, and Christ is the one it grasps. That is why the faith of verse 14 cannot save: it has words about Christ but has never closed on him. And no one can take hold of the Lord who went about doing good (Acts 10:38) and stay idle, any more than a branch joined to the vine can stay bare (John 15:5). The works James looks for are not a second hope beside Christ. They are the proof that Christ himself has been grasped.

What exactly is saving faith, then? Reformed teachers have long described it in three parts. Knowledge: knowing the truth about who Christ is and what he has done. Agreement: believing that it is true. And trust: resting on Christ personally, relying on him alone for forgiveness and life. The faith James attacks has the first two at most; it never comes to the third. True faith is like a drowning man taking hold of the rope. And a man who has taken hold of the rope does not stay in the water. He is pulled out, and his whole life moves in a new direction.

What about the thief on the cross? He had no time for good works. The thief was saved by faith alone, and his faith was alive. In his last hours it worked: he rebuked the other criminal, confessed his own guilt, defended Jesus’ innocence, and called on him as King (Luke 23:40–43). Works in James’s sense are not a quota to be filled before you qualify; they are the signs of life that appear wherever faith is real, however short the time. A newborn baby has not achieved anything, but it breathes and cries. So did the thief.
verseByVerse.note: Paul says we are justified by faith, not works; James says a faith that produces no works is not saving faith. They answer different errors.

verseByVerse.quote: If a brother or sister is poorly clothed and lacking in daily food, and one of you says to them, “Go in peace, be warmed and filled,” without giving them the things needed for the body, what good is that? So also faith by itself, if it does not have works, is dead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If a brother or sister is poorly clothed and lacking in daily food. The one in need is not a stranger but someone in the congregation. Brother or sister: James explicitly includes women. Poorly clothed means naked, inadequately dressed. And lacking in daily food means food for the day itself. This is not want of comfort. The person has nothing to eat today.

And one of you says to them, Go in peace, be warmed and filled. The words are entirely correct. Go in peace is the ordinary Jewish farewell blessing; the two verbs may even be the kind of wish used in prayer: “may you be warmed, may you be filled”. This is a man giving a genuine blessing and quite possibly praying.

Without giving them the things needed for the body. And there it is. He has said everything and done nothing, and the words themselves are what make it grotesque. Silence would have been less offensive. The words are kind; the absence of help is cruel.

What good is that? The same question as verse 14, and now with a cold answer available: the man is exactly as hungry as before, and has been sent away feeling blessed.

A coat and a meal. James could have picked adultery or theft to expose a hollow faith. He picks a coat and a meal, because the failure he describes is not scandalous: it is a religion that is fluent, warm, and costs nothing. John says the same: “let us not love in word or talk but in deed and in truth” (1 John 3:17–18).

So also faith by itself, if it does not have works, is dead. By itself means alone, on its own. Not weak, not immature, not needing something added. Dead, which is a word about what a thing is, not about how much of it there is. A corpse is not a person with reduced vitality. A faith that produces no works is not real, living faith.

What it does not mean. It does not mean faith becomes alive by adding works, as if works give life to faith. Rather, works show that faith is alive. A living tree bears fruit; the fruit does not make it alive.

But if my works are weak and inconsistent, is my faith dead? James is describing a faith with no works at all, words without a life behind them. He himself says we all stumble in many ways (3:2). Living faith may be small and imperfect, but it is real: it trusts Christ, it struggles against sin, and it shows itself, however feebly, in love.

Do I have to give to everyone who asks? James’s example is a brother or sister in the church, in real need, standing in front of you, and you able to help. Start there: your church family comes first (Galatians 6:10), and genuine need you can meet should be met. Beyond that, love uses wisdom. Sometimes giving money feeds an addiction, and a meal, a bag of shopping or a referral to the church’s care is better. Scripture also says that a man able to work but unwilling should not be fed for nothing (2 Thessalonians 3:10). Wisdom shapes how we help. It is never an excuse for not helping at all.

In everyday life. Is there someone you have wished well but not helped? Next time you say “I will pray for you”, consider whether you could also say: “And what can I bring round on Thursday?”

For worship. God did not send us away with a blessing. When we were naked and starving, he did not say “Go in peace, be warmed and filled.” He came. The Word became flesh and dwelt among us, fed the hungry with his own hands, and gave his body as bread for the life of the world. His love was never words only: “In this is love, not that we have loved God but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins” (1 John 4:10), the sacrifice that bore God’s just anger against our sin and turned it away from us. The gospel is not a well-wishing. It is a rescue, and every coat given in his name is a small picture of it.

verseByVerse.quote: But someone will say, “You have faith and I have works.” Show me your faith apart from your works, and I will show you my faith by my works. You believe that God is one; you do well. Even the demons believe—and shudder!
verseByVerse.commentary:
But someone will say, You have faith and I have works. James brings in an objector, and the punctuation of verse 18 has puzzled readers for centuries, since ancient manuscripts carried no quotation marks. The exact boundaries of the quotation are debated. The likeliest sense is someone saying: “These are two gifts. You have faith, and I have works. Different people, different strengths, and both are fine.” James rejects separating faith and works.

Show me your faith apart from your works. The reply is a challenge that cannot be met. Show means demonstrate, prove. It is unanswerable because faith is invisible. There is no way to display it except through what it does.

And I will show you my faith by my works. James, by contrast, can simply point to what he does. Works are the visible evidence of invisible faith. The only way to show faith is by its fruit; you will recognise them by their fruits (Matthew 7:16–20).

You believe that God is one; you do well. That is the Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4), recited by every devout Jew morning and evening, the foundation of the whole faith. James picks the soundest statement of belief there is and grants it fully: “you do well”. He is not belittling right belief.

Even the demons believe, and shudder! The demons believe in one God as firmly as anyone. Their theology is faultless; in Mark’s Gospel they name Jesus correctly while the crowds are still asking who he is: “I know who you are, the Holy One of God” (Mark 1:24; 5:7). So right belief (orthodoxy) cannot be the thing that distinguishes a Christian, because the demons have it and are not saved.

Orthodox and terrified. And the verb is worse than belief. They shudder: the hair standing on end. The creed is right and the feelings are real, and it changes nothing, because they do not trust, love or obey. That should search anyone whose Christianity consists of correct beliefs and real feelings in a service, and nothing more.

How do I know my faith is more than the demons’ faith? Ask what you do with what you believe. The demons know Jesus is the Son of God and want him to go away (Mark 5:7). Do you want him near? They tremble at God and hate him. Do you, even weakly, love him and want to please him? They believe, and keep on rebelling. Do you fight your sin, and grieve when you fail? Saving faith comes to Christ, rests on him, and wants to follow him. If that is the direction of your heart, however feeble, it is not demonic belief; it is the work of the Spirit.

The creed goes on to love. The demons hold the first line of the Shema and stop. But the Shema does not stop at “Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one.” It goes straight on: “You shall love the LORD your God with all your heart” (Deuteronomy 6:4–5). Saving faith believes the creed all the way into love, and the New Testament shows where that love is fixed: Paul restates the Shema with Christ inside it, one God, the Father, and one Lord, Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 8:6). The demons know who Jesus is. Only faith loves him. The God whose holiness makes devils shudder has opened his arms to sinners through his Son, and the Holy One of God whom the demons named in terror is the friend of sinners.

Should I look at my works to find assurance? Look first and chiefly to Christ: his promises, his finished work, his invitation to all who come. That is the foundation of assurance. Then your works and the change in your life serve as confirming evidence that your faith is real, and the Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God (Romans 8:16). The Westminster Confession (18.2) and the 1689 London Baptist Confession (18.2) teach the same. If you look only at your works, you will either become proud or despair. Look to Christ, and then you can look honestly at your life without fear, because your hope does not rest there.
verseByVerse.note: The confession “God is one” is the Shema, the daily creed of Israel.

verseByVerse.quote: Do you want to be shown, you foolish person, that faith apart from works is useless?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do you want to be shown, you foolish person. The address is sharp. “Want” means “are you willing”; “shown” means to know, recognise. And “foolish” means empty, hollow, vain. It is aimed at a religion that is only a claim, with nothing inside it, and it is a rebuke, not an insult: James means to fill what is empty, not to write the man off. God does not leave empty people empty. He fills the hungry with good things (Luke 1:53), and the Spirit he has poured into our hearts (Romans 5:5) is the one who turns idle faith into working love.

That faith apart from works is useless? Useless (argē) is a slight change from dead in verse 17. The word means idle, not working, out of employment. It is the term for land lying fallow or a labourer standing in the marketplace with nothing to do (Matthew 20:3). And there is a deliberate play in it: faith without works (ergōn) does not work (a-ergē). Some manuscripts read dead (as in vv. 17, 26), but useless is better supported; the KJV follows the later reading, faith without works is dead.

O foolish ones. The rebuke has a precedent that shows its purpose. On the Emmaus road the risen Jesus said, “O foolish ones, and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken!” and then, beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself (Luke 24:25–27). The sharp word opened the book, and the book opened onto him. James follows the same order: having argued from a scene and from the demons, he rebukes, then turns to Scripture, beginning with Abraham.

Jesus said whoever says You fool will be liable to judgment. Is James breaking that rule? No. Jesus was forbidding contemptuous insult flung in anger (Matthew 5:22). James is giving a pastoral diagnosis, the way Jesus himself called the Pharisees blind fools (Matthew 23:17) and the Emmaus disciples foolish. The difference is motive and purpose: the angry insult wants to wound and dismiss; the loving rebuke wants to wake someone up and bring him back. A friend who shouts as you step towards a cliff edge is not being cruel. James speaks sharply because the stakes are eternal.

verseByVerse.quote: Was not Abraham our father justified by works when he offered up his son Isaac on the altar? You see that faith was active along with his works, and faith was completed by his works;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Was not Abraham our father justified by works. This sentence needs facing directly. Abraham our father is the father of the Jewish people and of all who believe (Romans 4:11–12). James has chosen the same man Paul uses to prove justification by faith apart from works (Romans 4:1–5; Galatians 3:6), and appears to say the opposite. Justified here means shown to be righteous, vindicated, proved genuine, in the ordinary sense Jesus used when he said “wisdom is justified by her deeds” (Matthew 11:19), and that we use when we say events justified someone’s confidence.

When he offered up his son Isaac on the altar? The answer lies in the order of events, and James supplies it himself when he quotes Genesis 15:6 (v. 23). Abraham was counted righteous in Genesis 15, when he believed the promise about the stars. He offered Isaac in Genesis 22, many years later, probably decades. So the offering cannot be what made him righteous before God, since he had been counted righteous for years before he climbed the mountain. It demonstrated and vindicated his faith. God said afterward that now he knew Abraham feared him (Genesis 22:12). The test proved the faith genuine.

You see that faith was active along with his works. What then does justified by works mean here? Verse 22 answers exactly. Faith was active along with, working together with his works: collaborators, not rivals, and faith the active partner. Faith was the source; works were the expression.

And faith was completed by his works. Completed means brought to its intended end, matured, perfected, like fruit ripening. Not supplemented, but fulfilled, as a seed is fulfilled in a tree. Faith reached its full goal in obedience.

The faith that raised the knife. Moriah tested Abraham’s faith in the one place where it could be tested to destruction, since the son on the altar was the very promise he had believed God for. Only a man who genuinely trusted God to keep his word could raise that knife. Hebrews tells us what he was thinking: “He considered that God was able even to raise him from the dead” (Hebrews 11:17–19).

Does the story of Isaac mean God approves of child sacrifice? No. God stopped Abraham’s hand and provided the ram, and his law later condemned child sacrifice as an abomination (Leviticus 18:21; Jeremiah 7:31). The command was a unique test in the history of salvation, never to be repeated, and it was designed to point forward. In the land of Moriah, where Solomon later built the temple (2 Chronicles 3:1), not far from where Jesus would die, God would one day not spare his own Son (Romans 8:32). What God stopped Abraham from doing, he did himself, for us.

Will God test me the way he tested Abraham? Not with that command; it was unique, and God will never ask you to do what his word forbids. But he does test his people, asking whether we love him more than his gifts. Often the test comes in the thing we most treasure: a child, a career, a hope. God may ask you to hold it with an open hand, to trust him with it, to obey him when obedience seems to put it at risk. The lesson of Moriah is that God can be trusted with our Isaacs. The LORD will provide (Genesis 22:14). And if you have lost a child, hear this gently: your loss is not a test you failed or a price God demanded. The Father who did not spare his own Son knows that grief from the inside, and he is near to you in it.

For worship. On the mountain Isaac asked the question the whole Old Testament kept asking: the fire and the wood are here, but where is the lamb? (Genesis 22:7). Abraham answered that God would provide. The answer came by the Jordan, centuries later, when a prophet pointed to Jesus and said, “Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world” (John 1:29). The ram caught in the thicket died for one boy. The Lamb God provided died for all his people, and no voice from heaven stopped what was done to him. Abraham’s faith was completed by his works. Our salvation was completed by God’s.

verseByVerse.quote: and the Scripture was fulfilled that says, “Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness”—and he was called a friend of God. You see that a person is justified by works and not by faith alone.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the Scripture was fulfilled that says, Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness. Here James quotes Genesis 15:6, the very verse Paul builds Romans 4 on (Romans 4:3; Galatians 3:6). The statement stands; James is showing what happened to it afterwards. Counted means reckoned, credited, imputed: a legal and accounting word. God credited righteousness to Abraham when he believed. To impute is to put to someone’s account what was not his by nature, as a gift is paid into an empty bank account. Abraham did not have a righteous record to offer; God counted righteousness to him apart from works (Romans 4:6).

Fulfilled. And fulfilled is the key. The word is used of a prophecy coming true: filled up, brought to full meaning. God had declared Abraham righteous; on Moriah that declaration was shown to be true.

And he was called a friend of God. The title comes from 2 Chronicles 20:7 and Isaiah 41:8, and it is still how Abraham is known across the Middle East today: in Arabic, simply the Friend. Look at what James thinks the offering produced: not merit, but intimacy. The God of glory, who needs no one, calls such people his friends. Genuine faith leads to intimate relationship with God, shown in obedience; Jesus said, “You are my friends if you do what I command you” (John 15:14–15).

Counted for his sake and for ours. Paul draws out of the same verse what James assumes: the words it was counted to him were written not for Abraham’s sake alone, but for ours also, who believe in him who raised from the dead Jesus our Lord, who was delivered up for our trespasses and raised for our justification (Romans 4:23–25). The righteousness credited to a believing sinner is not his faith treated as a good work. It is Christ’s: for our sake God made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God (2 Corinthians 5:21). That is the root. Abraham on Moriah is the fruit, and James will not let us have one without the other.

You see that a person is justified by works and not by faith alone. The most debated phrase in James. It is the only place in the New Testament where the phrase “faith alone” appears, and here it is denied. But read what James actually denies. Justified here, as in verse 21, means shown or vindicated as righteous. Not by faith alone means not by the kind of faith described in verses 14–19: a faith that is on its own, unaccompanied, with nothing beside it, a mere profession. A person is shown to be righteous by works that prove the reality of their faith.

Where Christians differ: does this verse deny justification by faith alone? Roman Catholic teaching uses this verse as proof against the Reformation doctrine of justification by faith alone, and cites it to show that justification is a process of being made righteous, to which faith and works both contribute. Catholic teaching also insists that justification begins with God’s grace and not with human merit, and many Catholics sincerely love Christ; the disagreement is over what justification is. This commentary’s view: James is not denying that we are declared righteous by faith alone in Paul’s sense; he quotes Genesis 15:6 himself. He is not describing how a sinner is first accepted by God: he says that Abraham was counted righteous when he believed (v. 23), and then shows that faith proved true years later. He is denying that a faith which remains alone, without works, is saving faith. The Reformers said it well: we are justified by faith alone, but not by a faith that is alone. James and Paul agree: God declares sinners righteous by grace through faith in Christ, on the basis of his righteousness imputed to them; and the faith that receives this always works by love.

The counterfeit. James is not attacking the doctrine the Reformation recovered, justification by faith alone. He is attacking the counterfeit that always attaches itself to it. Every true doctrine has a cheap imitation, and the cheap imitation of justification by faith is a belief that costs nothing and changes nothing. James guards the real thing by exposing the fake.

If I stop doing good works, will I lose my justification? No. God’s verdict of justification is given once for all, rests entirely on Christ’s righteousness, and cannot be reversed: “those whom he justified he also glorified” (Romans 8:30). Those who are truly justified will persevere, because God keeps them (Philippians 1:6). A believer may go through dry and backslidden seasons and fall into serious sin, and he will be disciplined by his Father, but he will not finally fall away. If someone abandons Christ completely and permanently, it shows his faith was never the living kind (1 John 2:19). The answer to coldness is not fear of losing justification but returning to the Saviour who justified you.

Can I really be God’s friend? Yes. Abraham was a sinner who lied about his wife twice, and God called him friend. Jesus says to his disciples: “No longer do I call you servants … but I have called you friends” (John 15:15). Friendship with God is not reserved for spiritual giants; it is the privilege of everyone justified by faith. It means you may speak to him freely, share your heart, trust his heart, and enjoy his company. And it shows itself, as Abraham’s did, in trusting obedience.

Is it not a legal fiction for God to count a sinner righteous? It would be a fiction only if nothing real stood behind the verdict. But the righteousness counted to the believer is Christ’s, really lived in a perfect life and really paid for in a real death (2 Corinthians 5:21). Faith joins us to him, as a bride is joined to her husband, and what is his becomes ours: his name, his record, his standing with the Father. And the God who declares a sinner righteous never leaves him as he found him. The same Spirit who gives faith begins at once to make him new, which is exactly what James is insisting on.
verseByVerse.note: Abraham was counted righteous in Genesis 15, many years before he offered Isaac in Genesis 22; the offering showed the faith was real.

verseByVerse.quote: And in the same way was not also Rahab the prostitute justified by works when she received the messengers and sent them out by another way? For as the body apart from the spirit is dead, so also faith apart from works is dead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And in the same way was not also Rahab the prostitute justified by works. The second example is deliberately chosen to be as unlike the first as possible. Abraham is a man, the father of the nation, the patriarch, a Jew, the friend of God. Rahab is a woman, a Gentile, a Canaanite, and a prostitute, and James does not soften the noun. Between them they cover everybody. Genuine faith looks the same across every human distinction.

Two people God justified. And there may be a further point in a letter that has just condemned partiality: the congregation seating men by their clothes is shown two people God justified, one of whom they would not have let through the door. The church that would have sat her on the floor would have been snubbing a woman Matthew lists among King David’s ancestors.

When she received the messengers and sent them out by another way? Her work is specified. She “received” them, that is, welcomed them as guests; she hid the two spies under flax on her roof; and she “sent them out” (a strong word, thrust out) by a different route, so that they escaped (Joshua 2:1–21). It was treason against her own city, punishable by death, and it was done on the strength of what she had heard about Israel’s God: “the LORD your God, he is God in the heavens above and on the earth beneath” (Joshua 2:11). Her faith in Israel’s God led her to risk her life to protect his people. Her actions showed her faith was real. Hebrews 11:31 credits the same act to faith. James and Hebrews are looking at one event from two sides.

But Rahab lied. She lied to the king’s men (Joshua 2:4–5). James commends her faith, shown in receiving the spies and sending them out safely (Hebrews 11:31), not the lie as such. Christians differ on whether deceiving those bent on murder is a sin; either way, her faith was what God honoured, and ordinary lying is still sin.

The prostitutes go in first. Rahab’s place in the story is not an embarrassment the Bible tolerates; it is the gospel. Matthew names her in the family line of Jesus (Matthew 1:5). And Jesus told the chief priests that “the tax collectors and the prostitutes go into the kingdom of God before you”, because when John came, they believed him and you did not (Matthew 21:31–32). The Lord who came from her line came for her kind, and his kingdom is still entered the way she entered Israel.

For as the body apart from the spirit is dead. Spirit also means breath. A body without breath, without spirit, is a corpse.

So also faith apart from works is dead. The conclusion, repeating verse 17. Notice which is which: faith is the body, and works are the breath. Breath is what shows that a body is alive. James is saying that a faith with no works is a corpse: the shape is all there, the features are recognisable, and nothing is moving.

My past is like Rahab’s. Can my faith be real? Yes, and this verse was written partly for you. God did not wait for Rahab to clean up her reputation before he saved her. She believed with what little she knew, acted on it, and was brought into the people of God and into the family line of the Messiah. Your past does not limit what God can do with you; it magnifies his grace. The question is not where you have been but whom you are trusting now, and whether that trust is starting to move your hands and feet.

What does a living faith look like in an ordinary week? Usually it is quiet. It is the young mother who prays while she changes nappies and is patient with a toddler for Christ’s sake. It is the businessman who refuses the dishonest deal, the teenager who sits with the lonely kid at lunch, the old man who visits the hospital every Thursday, the couple who open their home to the church’s newcomers. Rahab’s work was one dangerous night, but most works of faith are small, repeated, and unseen. They are the breathing of a living faith, and breathing is rarely dramatic. It is only noticed when it stops.

For worship. When Jericho fell, a woman whose house was built into the wall, with a scarlet cord in its window, walked out alive with her family, with nothing to plead but faith (Joshua 6:22–25). That is how everyone comes out of the ruin. The Lord breathed his last on a cross for prostitutes and patriarchs alike, and on the third day he breathed again; on the evening of his rising he breathed on his disciples and said, “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20:22). Living faith breathes because the risen Christ has breathed into it, and what he has made alive he will never let die.
