3.title: The Tongue and True Wisdom
3.overview:
Chapter 3 deals with two linked themes: the tongue and wisdom. The tongue (vv. 1–12) is small but decisive, like a bit, a rudder or a spark, and no human can tame it. Its problem is not speech but the heart: a spring gives what its source supplies.

So James turns to wisdom (vv. 13–18). Earthly wisdom, full of jealousy and selfish ambition, produces disorder. Wisdom from above is pure, peaceable, gentle, open to reason, merciful, impartial and sincere, and it yields a harvest of righteousness sown in peace. The answer to the tongue is not a technique, but a new source.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A warning to would-be teachers opens onto the tongue itself: small but decisive, set on fire by hell, beyond human taming, and divided between blessing God and cursing the people who bear his likeness. The section ends by pointing past the words to their source.
verseByVerse.theology:
Why the Tongue Cannot Be Tamed

The tongue is small and decisive, and no human can tame it. The problem is the spring, not the water; the answer is wisdom from above.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Too many in the congregation wanted to teach.

Now: We cannot bless God and curse people made in his likeness from the same mouth.

verseByVerse.quote: Not many of you should become teachers, my brothers, for you know that we who teach will be judged with greater strictness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. James 3 takes up two themes from chapter 1, the tongue (1:19, 26) and wisdom (1:5): the small, untameable tongue that blesses God and curses people made in his likeness (vv. 1–12), and the two wisdoms that lie behind our words (vv. 13–18). The chapter that begins with a fire set by hell ends with a harvest sown from heaven.

Not many of you. A startling opening, and it tells us that too many in that congregation wanted the job. Teachers held a recognised and respected role (Acts 13:1). In a Jewish setting the rabbi was among the most honoured figures in the community, and in scattered congregations with no settled structure the man who could hold a room had an obvious opportunity.

We who teach. James puts himself inside the warning, the only honest way to issue it. Greater strictness is literally a greater judgment, a principle that runs through Scripture: to whom much is given, much is required (Luke 12:48). A teacher handles other people’s souls with his words, and error from the front does damage that error in private conversation does not. Teachers answer both for what they teach and for how they live (Matthew 12:36–37), because their hearers copy both.

The wanting. This is not discouragement of the gift, which the New Testament commands and prizes. What James discourages is the wanting: the drift toward a visible role for reasons that have more to do with standing than with service.

You have one teacher. James’s warning echoes his brother’s. Do not be called rabbi, Jesus said, for you have one teacher, and you are all brothers; you have one instructor, the Christ (Matthew 23:8–10). Every teacher in the church is a pupil first, under the one Teacher, who will never be judged, because he is the Judge, and whose words were never once careless. “No one ever spoke like this man!” (John 7:46). A church teacher’s authority is borrowed, and only as good as his faithfulness to what Christ has said. That is what makes the greater strictness fair. He handles words that are not his, about a Lord who will ask how he handled them.

I teach Sunday school, lead a small group, or teach my children. Should this verse frighten me off? It should sober you, not silence you. If God has given you the opportunity and the church has entrusted it to you, do it gladly. Parents are commanded to teach their children (Deuteronomy 6:6–7). The warning is for the person who wants the platform more than the people, and for anyone careless with God’s truth. So prepare properly, teach only what Scripture says, admit what you do not know, live what you teach, and let your church’s elders correct you. The greater strictness is a reason for care, not for fear: the same Lord who will judge teachers is the one who forgives them.

How should I choose whom to listen to, especially online? With the same seriousness James shows. Not every confident voice is a qualified one. Ask: does this teacher explain the Bible, or use it for his own ideas? Is his life consistent with his teaching? Is he accountable to a local church and its elders? Does his teaching make Christ great and make you more humble, holy and loving, or more angry, proud and suspicious? And do not let any online teacher replace the pastor who knows your name and will give account for your soul (Hebrews 13:17).

verseByVerse.quote: For we all stumble in many ways. And if anyone does not stumble in what he says, he is a perfect man, able also to bridle his whole body.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We all stumble. The verb (as in 2:10) is the ordinary word for tripping: not falling headlong, but catching your foot. It happens many times, in many areas, to everyone, and mostly without intention. James, the pillar of the Jerusalem church, says we.

A perfect man. Perfect is teleios again, as in 1:4: mature, complete. James is not describing sinlessness but full growth, and the case is hypothetical, since we all stumble. But it gives a very practical test: speech is the reliable measure of maturity. Not doctrine, zeal, attendance or even generosity, all of which can be produced by effort or temperament. The tongue is often the last thing to come under control, so a man who has it in hand has everything else in hand.

Why speech tells the truth. Much of what we say is not chosen beforehand; it simply comes out, which makes it the most honest evidence available about what is actually inside. What comes out when you are tired, interrupted or contradicted is a fair sample of what is in there.

His whole body. James is not saying the tongue is the worst part of a person but the controlling part, the test of self-control.

The one perfect man. There has been one such man. “He committed no sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth. When he was reviled, he did not revile in return” (1 Peter 2:22–23). Every word Jesus spoke was true and well-timed, all the way to a cross where he said, “Father, forgive them” (Luke 23:34). The maturity James describes has a name, and his righteousness, words included, is counted to us who stumble in ours.

Where Christians differ: can a Christian stop stumbling altogether in this life? Some holiness and Wesleyan traditions teach that believers can attain entire sanctification, a state of freedom from conscious sin; they rightly long for a heart wholly given to love, and many of them are earnest, godly people. This commentary’s view: James says we all stumble in many ways, including himself, an apostolic leader. Scripture teaches that believers grow in holiness throughout life but are never sinless until glory (1 John 1:8–10; Philippians 3:12–14; Romans 7:14–25). We pursue maturity earnestly, but we always need daily forgiveness.

What counts as stumbling in speech? More than swearing. Scripture names lying, exaggeration, gossip and slander, flattery, boasting, grumbling and complaining, harsh and cutting words, sarcasm meant to wound, crude joking, breaking promises, and careless words spoken in anger (Ephesians 4:25–31; 5:4; Philippians 2:14). It also includes what we fail to say: the encouragement withheld, the truth not spoken, the apology not made. Most of us stumble daily. The point is not to despair but to notice, confess, and ask God to make our words like his.

In everyday life. Keep a quiet watch on your words for one day: not to scold yourself, but to learn. Mark when you exaggerated, interrupted, complained or spoke sharply, and what was happening at the time. At the end of the day, confess them specifically, and where someone was hurt, put it right before you sleep. The mouth that never stumbled is speaking for you: he always lives to make intercession for those who stumble daily (Hebrews 7:25), and his one word for us outweighs all our careless ones.

verseByVerse.quote: If we put bits into the mouths of horses so that they obey us, we guide their whole bodies as well. Look at the ships also: though they are so large and are driven by strong winds, they are guided by a very small rudder wherever the will of the pilot directs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Bits into the mouths of horses. Two illustrations make the same point from opposite ends of ordinary experience. A horse weighs half a ton and can kill a man; the bit is a few ounces of iron, and the disproportion is the whole argument. Control the mouth, control the horse.

The ships also. Same disproportion, with an added factor: the ship is not merely large, it is under enormous pressure from the gales.

A very small rudder. A steering oar at the stern still decides where it goes. Both images say the same thing about the tongue: small, and decisive. It is not one member among many. It is the helm.

Who has the rudder? There is a detail in the second picture: wherever the will of the pilot (euthynontos, the one steering) directs. The rudder is small and powerful, and it is also steered. It does not choose the course; somebody’s intention is behind it. That is the hopeful note in a chapter that is about to turn very dark. If the tongue is a rudder, the question is who has hold of it. James will say shortly that no human being can tame it, but a rudder was never meant to be tamed. It was meant to be steered. The winds that drive our lives are strong, but there is a Pilot who has never lost a ship. He who rebuked the wind and calmed the sea (Mark 4:39) can calm the tongue, and bring every one of his people safe into harbour.

A tongue that says Jesus is Lord. If the tongue is a rudder, the gospel answers the question of who holds it. The first thing a Christian’s mouth does as a Christian is confess: “if you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved” (Romans 10:9). And no one can say “Jesus is Lord” except in the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:3). The rudder has changed hands. A tongue that has once said Jesus is Lord is meant to go on saying it in every sentence after.

Does this mean I can steer my life by speaking positive words over it? No. Some teachers claim that our words have creative power, so that by declaring health or wealth we bring it into being. That is not what James means, and it is not biblical. Only God speaks things into existence. James means that our words steer our relationships and our character: a habit of complaining steers a life toward bitterness, a habit of lying toward ruin, a habit of encouragement and prayer toward peace. Our words do not command God; they reveal and shape us.

In everyday life. Your words are steering your closest relationships toward warmth or toward distance. Since the rudder is now in Christ’s hand, choose one relationship where you will deliberately steer with kindness this week.

verseByVerse.quote: So also the tongue is a small member, yet it boasts of great things. How great a forest is set ablaze by such a small fire! And the tongue is a fire, a world of unrighteousness. The tongue is set among our members, staining the whole body, setting on fire the entire course of life, and set on fire by hell.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Such a small fire. The bit and the rudder were neutral instruments; a fire is not. James has moved from the tongue’s power to its danger, and every image from here is destructive. A spark, and a hillside of brushwood is gone. The disproportion is the same as before, but now the small thing does great harm. A single careless word can destroy a reputation, a friendship, a marriage, a church.

A world of unrighteousness. Verse 6 is ferocious: a whole universe of wrong contained in one organ, lies, slander, gossip, flattery, boasting, cursing, false teaching.

Staining the whole body. Staining is the opposite of the unstained of 1:27. What we say defiles our whole person: what comes out of the mouth proceeds from the heart, and this defiles a person (Matthew 15:11, 18).

The entire course of life. Literally “the wheel of birth”, an unusual phrase perhaps borrowed from popular philosophy: the whole revolving round of a person’s existence, alight from end to end.

Set on fire by hell. The word is Gehenna, the word Jesus used for final punishment (Mark 9:43–48). Gehenna was the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, once defiled by child sacrifice (2 Kings 23:10; Jeremiah 7:31), later a symbol of God’s judgment. James is saying that destructive speech has a supply line, and it runs from below: its source is in hell itself, in Satan, the father of lies (John 8:44).

Why James goes so far. The reason for such strong words is probably in his congregation: these were people under pressure, poor, scattered and quarrelling (4:1), and what was doing them most harm seems to have been not persecution from outside but what they were saying to each other.

Tongues set on fire from heaven. James names the supply line of destructive speech, and the gospel names another. At Pentecost divided tongues as of fire rested on the disciples, and what came out of their mouths was the mighty works of God (Acts 2:3–4, 11). The same Peter who seven weeks earlier had called down curses and sworn that he did not know the man (Mark 14:71) now preached him to thousands. A tongue lit from hell is not put out by effort. It is relit from above by the ascended Christ, so that tongues which once spread poison might spend eternity in praise.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the tongue can only do evil: “death and life are in the power of the tongue” (Proverbs 18:21). And the word Gehenna does not mean that the Valley of Hinnom is itself the place of final punishment; the valley gave its name to the real, conscious, eternal punishment of the wicked.

When I lose my temper and say terrible things, is that the devil? It is your own sin, for which you are responsible, and the devil is glad to fan it. James does not say every harsh word is demonic possession; he says destructive speech serves the devil’s purposes and draws on his fire. That should make us take our words very seriously, and it should also make us run to Christ, who has defeated the devil (Hebrews 2:14). You do not fight hell’s fire with willpower. You fight it with confession, the word of God and the Spirit’s help.

I have already started a fire with my words. What do I do? Act quickly, because fires spread. Go to the person you hurt, privately, and say plainly what you said and that it was wrong, without excuses or blaming. If you spread gossip, go back to those you told and correct it. Ask forgiveness from God and from them. Do what you can to restore the reputation you damaged. You cannot unsay words, but honest repentance can stop a fire spreading and often begins to heal what was burned. And God can rebuild what our tongues have destroyed.

In everyday life. Before you post or send a message, ask whether it will light a fire, and whether you would say it to the person’s face with Christ standing beside you.
verseByVerse.note: “Hell” here translates Gehenna, the word Jesus used for final judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: For every kind of beast and bird, of reptile and sea creature, can be tamed and has been tamed by mankind, but no human being can tame the tongue. It is a restless evil, full of deadly poison.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every kind of beast and bird. The four kinds of creature echo Genesis 1:26 and 9:2: the rule over the animals that God gave to Adam (his dominion) has actually been carried out.

No human being can tame. The sentence the chapter has been building toward: man rules the animal creation and cannot rule six inches of his own mouth. The claim is absolute and should not be softened into “it is difficult”. It cannot be done, not by resolve, not by technique, not by the wisdom of a long life. Only God can (Proverbs 16:1).

A restless evil. The same word he used of the double-minded man in 1:8: like a wild animal pacing in a cage, never at rest, always ready to break out.

Deadly poison. The image is the snake, like the poison of asps under their lips (Psalm 140:3; Romans 3:13). A snake is rarely tamed; at best its venom is drawn. And the tongue is not occasionally venomous but full of it.

Why James shuts the door. James is not writing a self-improvement chapter. He shuts that door deliberately, and the chapter’s answer, when it comes at verse 17, is not a technique for controlling speech but a wisdom from above. The problem is not the mouth. It never was.

But we see Jesus. The dominion over beasts, birds and fish is also the theme of Psalm 8:6–8. Man has exercised it, and the one thing he cannot rule is himself. Hebrews reads the same psalm and admits the gap: we do not yet see everything in subjection to him. But we see Jesus, crowned with glory and honour because of the suffering of death (Hebrews 2:8–9). No human being can tame the tongue, but the Son of God became a human being and did. He who spoke the stars into being learned to speak as a child in Nazareth, and never once let poison pass his lips. The dominion lost in Adam has been recovered in one man, who ruled his own tongue perfectly, and he rules ours now by his Spirit.

If no one can tame the tongue, what can a Christian do? No human being can tame it, but God can change the heart from which words come (Matthew 12:34). Pray: “Set a guard, O LORD, over my mouth” (Psalm 141:3); fill the heart with God’s word; think before speaking; and when the tongue fails, confess and make it right. The Spirit’s fruit includes self-control (Galatians 5:23).

If I cannot tame my tongue, how can God blame me for what it says? Because the inability is not like a broken leg; it is in the will. Nobody forces the cutting remark out of us. We say it because, at that moment, we want to, and James goes on to show that the words come up from what the heart loves (3:11; Matthew 12:34). A man who cannot stop lying because he loves himself more than the truth is not less guilty for it, but more. That is why the answer is not an excuse but a new heart, and why the holy God who holds us responsible is also the God who gives the Spirit to those who ask him (Luke 11:13).

What if someone’s words have poisoned me, and I still hear them years later? Poisonous words from a parent, a spouse, a teacher or a church leader can do deep harm, and Scripture takes that seriously; this whole passage says so. Bring those words to God and set them beside what he says about you in Christ: chosen, forgiven, loved, his child. Let his word answer theirs, again and again, until his voice is louder. Talk to a wise pastor or counsellor if the wound is deep. And if the person is still harming you with words, that is not something you must simply endure; seek help and protection.

verseByVerse.quote: With it we bless our Lord and Father, and with it we curse people who are made in the likeness of God. From the same mouth come blessing and cursing. My brothers, these things ought not to be so.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We bless our Lord and Father. This is the double-mindedness of 1:8 in its most visible form, and the pronoun once more is we. Lord and Father together is found only here in the New Testament; most later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, read God, even the Father. The blessing is genuine; the same mouth was singing an hour ago. That is what makes the charge land: he is describing not hypocrites who despise God, but worshippers.

The likeness of God. To curse is to call down evil on someone. The argument turns on one phrase, “made in the likeness of God”. The Greek tense means made so, and still bearing it. James reaches back to Genesis 1:26–27, and so makes cursing a person an offence against God, not merely an unkind act. Every human being bears God’s image, even after the fall (Genesis 9:6), and to curse a person is to insult the God whose image they bear. To bear his image means that every person was made to reflect God: to know him and love him, to think, choose and create, and to look after his world on his behalf (Genesis 1:26–28), rather as a king’s statue in a distant province shows whose land it is. Sin has defaced that likeness but never erased it, so the man you are tempted to curse still carries, however dimly, the marks of his Maker.

The original and the image. You cannot bless the original and curse the image; one of the two acts must be insincere. It is the argument of 1 John 4:20 in other terms: “he who does not love his brother whom he has seen cannot love God whom he has not seen”. And note the scope. James does not say we curse our enemies, or the wicked. He says “people”. It covers the difficult neighbour, the political opponent, and the person in the congregation who has genuinely wronged you.

The Image they cursed. The argument reaches its sharpest point at the cross. Every person bears God’s likeness, but one man is the image of the invisible God (Colossians 1:15), and men cursed him to his face. Those who passed by derided him, and the chief priests and scribes, men who blessed God in their prayers, mocked him as he died (Mark 15:29–32). Every contemptuous word about a person made in God’s likeness is a small echo of that afternoon.

These things ought not to be so. A remarkably restrained conclusion after the fire of verse 6, and addressed to brothers. It is a real rebuke, because this double-tongued behaviour is incompatible with genuine faith. But James thunders about the tongue in the abstract and speaks softly to the people who have one.

Is all cursing forbidden, then? The psalms and prophets call down God’s judgment on his enemies, and Paul says a false gospel is accursed (Galatians 1:8). That is leaving judgment to God. What James forbids is cursing people out of malice in our own name; Jesus calls his disciples to “bless those who curse you” (Luke 6:28).

What about swearing and crude language? Scripture says: “Let no corrupting talk come out of your mouths, but only such as is good for building up” (Ephesians 4:29), and it rules out filthiness, foolish talk and crude joking (Ephesians 5:4). Using God’s name carelessly breaks the third commandment. Crude and obscene speech cheapens what God made good. But the deeper issue James raises is not vocabulary but contempt. A man can avoid every rude word and still destroy someone with a polite sentence. Watch both: the words, and the heart behind them.

Can I criticise politicians and public figures? Yes, you may disagree with their policies and actions, even strongly, and speak truthfully about wrongdoing. But they too bear God’s image, and we are commanded to pray for those in authority (1 Timothy 2:1–2) and to honour everyone (1 Peter 2:17). Mockery, slander, sharing half-truths and wishing them harm are what James forbids. A useful test: would you be comfortable if they heard what you said, and if Christ heard it too?

In everyday life. Take the person you have spoken of most harshly this month and bring them before God: ask him to bless them, and then say one true and good thing about them to someone else.

verseByVerse.quote: Does a spring pour forth from the same opening both fresh and salt water? Can a fig tree, my brothers, bear olives, or a grapevine produce figs? Neither can a salt pond yield fresh water.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Does a spring pour forth from the same opening both fresh and salt water? Three questions from nature, and each expects the answer no. The picture is local and vivid. A spring (pēgē) in dry Palestine was precious, and around the Dead Sea and the Jordan valley there are both sweet springs and brackish ones, and no one confuses them. A spring is defined by what comes out of its opening (opē, crack, hole), and what comes out is determined by what it draws from. A spring gives one kind of water; it cannot give both sweet and bitter.

Can a fig tree, my brothers, bear olives, or a grapevine produce figs? The same logic holds among plants: each plant produces according to its kind (Genesis 1:11–12). And the Lord had made the identical point: you will recognise them by their fruits; are grapes gathered from thornbushes? (Matthew 7:16–20; 12:33–35).

A salt pond. The final line rules out any softer reading. A salt spring like those near the Dead Sea could not produce drinkable water, not even occasionally. A spring that gives both kinds of water is not merely inconsistent but impossible. So when blessing and cursing come from the same mouth, something is wrong at the source.

Deal with the spring. All three pictures say that the output reveals the source, and no tree or spring has ever been talked into producing something foreign to it. That answers the question the previous verses raise: if no human can tame the tongue, what is to be done? You do not work on the water. You deal with the spring. Speech is a symptom.

A new spring. Jesus made the same diagnosis: make the tree good and its fruit good, for out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks (Matthew 12:33–34). And he did more than diagnose. To a Samaritan woman he promised water that will become in him “a spring of water welling up to eternal life” (John 4:14), and at the feast he cried, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink”, speaking, John explains, of the Spirit (John 7:37–39). The source can be changed, and he is the one who changes it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean a believer who sometimes speaks sinfully is not a believer. We all stumble (v. 2). It means the pattern of our speech reveals the nature of our heart (Luke 6:45). A heart renewed by God will increasingly produce good speech; persistent evil speech reveals an unrenewed heart.

So how does the spring actually change? Only God can change a heart, and he does it through the gospel and his Spirit. In practice, that means feeding the spring: filling your mind with Scripture, so that his words are what flow out (Colossians 3:16); confessing the bitterness, envy or fear underneath the words, not just the words themselves; and praying for a clean heart (Psalm 51:10). Ask what is behind your harshest words. Usually it is pride, hurt, or fear. Take that to Christ. Sweet water comes from a heart that has been forgiven much and knows it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: James answers the tongue with wisdom, and sets two kinds side by side: the counterfeit, driven by envy and ambition and leaving disorder behind it, and the wisdom from above, known almost entirely by how it treats people.
verseByVerse.theology:
Wisdom Shown, Not Stated

Wisdom is proved by good conduct in meekness. The wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceable, and almost every mark of it concerns how we treat others.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Bitter jealousy and selfish ambition lay behind the quarrelling.

Now: The eagerness to be seen as wise is itself evidence against the claim.

verseByVerse.quote: Who is wise and understanding among you? By his good conduct let him show his works in the meekness of wisdom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who is wise and understanding among you? The question returns to verse 1 and the men who wanted to teach. Very well: here is how the claim is tested. Wise (sophos) is one who has practical, godly wisdom; understanding (epistēmōn) is knowledgeable, expert, skilful.

By his good conduct. The test is not what you would expect: not an examination, not a doctrinal statement, not fluency. Good conduct is literally a beautiful way of life. Wisdom in the Bible is skill in living, so the evidence for it is a life rather than an argument. A man may be able to explain wisdom faultlessly and not have any.

The meekness of wisdom. This phrase is the one that stings. Meekness, as in 1:21, is not timidity but strength under control: a word Greek writers are said to have used of a tamed horse, all the power still there and now answering the rein. The genuinely wise man is not pushing. He does not need to win the room or be recognised as the wisest person in it, and in a congregation where too many wanted to teach, the eagerness to be seen as wise is itself evidence against the claim.

Learn from me. The quality James names is the one Jesus claimed for himself: “learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart” (Matthew 11:29). The school of heavenly wisdom has one master, and its first lesson is his meekness. That is why the eager would-be teacher is not yet wise: he has not sat at the feet of the gentle one long enough to stop pushing.

How can I tell whether a church leader or teacher is truly wise? Look at the life, not only the gifts. Is he humble and teachable? Does he listen before he speaks? How does he treat people who cannot help him, the elderly, children, the awkward, the critic? Is his home in order? How does he handle being contradicted? Paul’s lists of qualifications for elders are mostly about character, not ability (1 Timothy 3:1–7; Titus 1:5–9). A brilliant speaker who is harsh, proud and quarrelsome is not wise, however impressive he sounds.

Isn’t meekness just weakness? Not in Scripture. Moses confronted Pharaoh and was called the meekest man on earth. Jesus overturned the money-changers’ tables and called himself gentle and lowly. Meekness is power yielded to God: strong enough to fight, humble enough not to fight for itself. The meek person can stand firm on the truth and still be gentle in manner, can be wronged without retaliating, and can lose an argument without losing his peace. That takes more strength, not less.

In everyday life. In your next disagreement, at home, at work or in church, be the one who asks questions and listens, and does not need to have the last word.

For worship. The wisest man who ever lived was meek. One greater than Solomon came (Matthew 12:42), and he showed his wisdom not by dazzling the learned but by washing feet. He confounded the scholars at twelve and spent the next years in a carpenter’s shop. He could silence his enemies with a sentence, and he did not open his mouth before his accusers. In him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Colossians 2:3), and he spent them on fishermen.

verseByVerse.quote: But if you have bitter jealousy and selfish ambition in your hearts, do not boast and be false to the truth. This is not the wisdom that comes down from above, but is earthly, unspiritual, demonic. For where jealousy and selfish ambition exist, there will be disorder and every vile practice.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Bitter jealousy and selfish ambition. Two words name what was actually happening. Jealousy is zēlos, zeal, which can be a virtue and here is bitter, like the salt water of verse 11: passion for a cause curdled into passion against a person. Selfish ambition is a rare word used before the New Testament of self-seeking in politics: working a crowd for your own advancement.

In your hearts. This is the spring of verse 11. The quarrelling tongues have a source, and James has found it.

False to the truth. To claim to be wise while this is going on inside you is not merely mistaken; it is a lie told about reality.

Earthly, unspiritual, demonic. Then the verdict, in three descending words. Earthly: it belongs to this world and reaches no higher. Unspiritual, literally soulish: merely human powers of mind and feeling, working without the Spirit (1 Corinthians 2:14; Jude 19). And demonic, where the descent ends: its ultimate source is the devil, whose original sin Scripture links with pride (1 Timothy 3:6).

Disorder and every vile practice. Disorder is upheaval, confusion, the same word family as the restless tongue of verse 8 and the unstable man of 1:8. The private ambition produces public chaos, and the chaos then makes room for everything else.

The wisdom that crucified the Lord of glory. James’s analysis was once proved on a public scale. Pilate knew that it was out of envy that they had delivered him up (Matthew 27:18). Fear for their place became a plot (John 11:48), the plot a trial with false witnesses, and the disorder ended with a crowd demanding a murderer’s release. None of the rulers of this age understood God’s wisdom, Paul says, for if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory (1 Corinthians 2:8). Selfish ambition sat among his own disciples at the Last Supper, arguing about which of them was the greatest, and he answered envy and ambition alike by taking a towel and dying on a cross. The one with every right to ambition laid it down. Earthly, unspiritual, demonic: that wisdom killed Christ, and God turned its worst act into the salvation of the world.

What it does not mean. It does not condemn all ambition. Wanting to serve God well and use our gifts fully is good: “earnestly desire the higher gifts” (1 Corinthians 12:31), and “If anyone aspires to the office of overseer, he desires a noble task” (1 Timothy 3:1). It condemns selfish ambition, which seeks one’s own glory at others’ expense.

How do I fight envy when a friend succeeds where I have not? Name it honestly before God; envy hides behind criticism and loves to call itself discernment. Remember that God gives his gifts as he wills, and that your worth is not set by comparison but by his love for you in Christ. Then do the opposite of what envy wants: thank God for your friend’s blessing, pray for them, and tell them you are glad. “Rejoice with those who rejoice” (Romans 12:15). Feelings often follow obedience. And look at what God has given you, because envy blinds us to our own gifts.

Our church is in conflict, and I think ambition is behind it. What should I do? Start with your own heart: is there any selfish ambition or bitterness in you? Then refuse to feed the fire: do not gossip, take sides on social media, or spread rumours. If you have a concern, take it privately and humbly to the person or to the elders (Matthew 18:15). Pray for the leaders and for peace. Be a peacemaker, not a party member. If there is real sin or abuse, it must be dealt with properly and openly, not covered up. Truth and peace together are the goal.

verseByVerse.quote: But the wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, open to reason, full of mercy and good fruits, impartial and sincere. And a harvest of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
First pure. Now the answer to the whole chapter: not a technique for controlling the tongue, which James has said cannot be done, but a wisdom from the same direction as every good gift (1:17), offered to anyone who asks (1:5). It is not achieved; it is given. First means first in priority, the foundation of the others. Pure means holy, without mixed motives.

Then peaceable. The order is deliberate. Purity is not negotiable, and it comes before peaceableness, which forbids the false peace that keeps quiet about sin to avoid trouble. But having secured the order, James lets peace govern everything after it, the opposite of the jealousy and disorder of verses 14–16.

Gentle. The word is epieikēs, almost untranslatable: gracious, considerate, forbearing, the man who does not insist on the last inch of his rights. It is a qualification for elders (1 Timothy 3:3).

Open to reason. Easily persuaded, willing to yield, teachable: an extraordinary thing to require of wisdom, and exactly what the quarrelling teachers lacked.

Full of mercy and good fruits. Mercy is compassion in action, as in 2:13, and good fruits are the works that show faith is alive (2:14–26).

Impartial. The word means without wavering, undivided, unprejudiced. It reaches back both to chapter 2 and the gold ring, not showing favouritism (2:1–9), and to chapter 1, not double-minded (1:6–8).

Sincere. Without a mask, not play-acting: the opposite of the double-mindedness that has run through the whole letter.

What the list leaves out. Not one of these qualities is about cleverness: heavenly wisdom is described almost entirely by how a person treats others. And read with Jesus in view, the list is a portrait, for he became to us wisdom from God (1 Corinthians 1:30). Pure: he knew no sin. Gentle: a bruised reed he did not break. Open to reason: he answered honest questions patiently, from Nicodemus by night to doubting Thomas. Full of mercy and good fruits: he went about doing good. Impartial: he ate with Pharisees and with tax collectors. Sincere: no deceit was found in his mouth. The wisdom from above has a face.

A harvest of righteousness. The metaphor closes the chapter that opened with fire. Fire destroys in an afternoon; sowing produces slowly and only in the right conditions. And the peacemakers are not merely those who avoid conflict but those who make peace, which is work, and which is what the whole congregation had stopped doing. “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matthew 5:9).

Does open to reason mean I should change my convictions whenever someone disagrees? No. Wisdom is first pure; it does not bend on what God has clearly said. But on everything else, and on how we hold what God has said, it is willing to listen, to learn, and to admit error. The wise person can say: “I had not thought of that; you may be right; I was wrong.” The foolish person cannot. One test: if you hold your own opinions as firmly as you hold God’s word, you have probably confused the two.

How do I actually make peace? Begin by being at peace with God through Christ, because peacemakers are those who have been reconciled (Romans 5:1). Then go first: do not wait for the other person to come to you (Matthew 5:23–24). Listen to understand, not to win. Own your part honestly, without adding “but”. Speak the truth gently. Look for what you can agree on. If two other believers are in conflict, do not carry stories between them; help them talk to each other, or bring in a wise elder. And keep sowing: peace often grows slowly, like a harvest.

In everyday life. Go down the list, pick the quality you most lack, and ask God for it, as he promised (1:5).

For worship. The wisdom from above came down. It lay in a manger and hung on a cross, and there the great Peacemaker made peace by the blood of his cross (Colossians 1:20), sowing himself in the ground like a seed so that a harvest of righteousness could rise from his grave. He is our peace (Ephesians 2:14), and the wisdom that came down is still given to everyone who asks.

4.title: Submit to God: Pride, the World, and the Brevity of Life
4.overview:
Chapter 4 goes to the root of the church’s failures. Quarrels come from desires at war within each person. Those desires come from friendship with the world, which is spiritual adultery against God. The remedy is humble submission to God. At the centre stands Proverbs 3:34: “God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble.” And “he gives more grace.”

The chapter ends with two warnings against taking God’s place: judging a brother, which sets us over the law, and planning as if tomorrow were ours, which forgets that we are a mist. The humble say, “If the Lord wills.”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — Quarrels, Adultery, and More Grace
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: James traces the congregation’s quarrels to desires at war within, and names their loyalty to the world as adultery against God. Then the turn: God gives more grace to the humble, and ten urgent commands spell out what it is to come to him low.
verseByVerse.theology:
But He Gives More Grace

Quarrels come from desires at war within us, and friendship with the world is spiritual adultery. Yet God gives more grace to the humble.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The readers prayed, but to fund the very desires that divided them.

Now: Submit to God, resist the devil, draw near, and he will draw near to you.

verseByVerse.quote: What causes quarrels and what causes fights among you? Is it not this, that your passions are at war within you? You desire and do not have, so you murder. You covet and cannot obtain, so you fight and quarrel. You do not have, because you do not ask.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. James 4 traces conflict to its root and calls for humble repentance. Quarrels come from desires at war within (vv. 1–3); friendship with the world is adultery against God (vv. 4–5); and at the centre stands the sentence that turns everything: “But he gives more grace” (v. 6). Ten commands follow for coming to him low (vv. 7–10), then two more faces of pride: judging a brother (vv. 11–12) and boasting about tomorrow (vv. 13–17).

What causes quarrels and what causes fights among you? James asks it the way a doctor asks where the pain is: to find the cause. Quarrels (polemoi, wars, battles) and fights (machai, conflicts, disputes) are military words for church conflicts. Chapter 3 traced the quarrelling tongues to jealousy and selfish ambition in the heart (3:14–16); now he goes deeper still.

Is it not this, that your passions are at war within you? The word is hēdonai, pleasures, desires for pleasure, from which we get hedonism. At war (strateuomenōn) means waging a military campaign. And the location is “within you”, literally “in your members”, the parts of your own body. The war is not between the factions in the congregation. It is within each person, and the fighting outside is that inner war showing. Desires fight against God and against each other within us (Romans 7:23; 1 Peter 2:11).

The quarrel is only the symptom. A man at war inside himself will find something to fight about outside, and if you settle the question he is arguing about, he will find another. The music, the building, the rota, the budget: these are rarely the real war. They are only where it broke out.

So you murder. Verse 2 packs a great deal into few words. The word “murder” has troubled readers, and some have suggested that James really wrote “envy”, but the manuscripts do not support it. More likely James is doing what his brother did in the Sermon on the Mount: tracing sin to its root, where hatred is already murder (Matthew 5:21–22; 1 John 3:15). He is not accusing them of homicide but naming where the desire is heading: hatred, character assassination, destroying others with words, as unchecked desire led Cain.

You covet. The pattern comes twice: desire, frustration, violence. The violence is not the root problem; it is what desire does when it is blocked.

Because you do not ask. After all that heat, the simplest possible sentence. They have organised their whole inner life around getting, and it has not occurred to them to ask the God who gives generously to all without reproach (1:5). We try to grab what God would give if we asked.

Grasping or asking. Behind the quarrel lies a lie about God: that what he withholds must be seized. James answers it with the teaching of Jesus, who said, “Ask, and it will be given to you”, and “how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him!” (Matthew 7:7–11). And Jesus lived it. Though he was in the form of God, he did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped (Philippians 2:6); and the Father’s word to him was, “Ask of me, and I will make the nations your heritage” (Psalm 2:8). The church fights because it grasps. Its Lord, who alone had the right to take, asked. In him there was no war within: he desired one thing above all, his Father’s will, and every other desire was ordered under it. The war inside us will not end by our own resolve. It ends at the feet of the Prince of Peace.

What it does not mean. It does not mean all desire is wrong: “Delight yourself in the LORD, and he will give you the desires of your heart” (Psalm 37:4). The problem is desire for pleasure that rules us and sets us against others.

But surely some church conflicts are about real issues, like truth? Yes. Some disagreements are about the gospel itself, and then faithfulness requires standing firm (Jude 3; Galatians 2:11). But even then James’s question is worth asking: what is going on in me? It is possible to be right about the issue and wrong in the heart, fighting for truth with pride, anger and a desire to win. And most church quarrels, honestly examined, are not about the gospel at all but about preferences, status and being heard. Ask God to show you which yours is.

Does you do not ask mean that if I pray I will get whatever I want? No. The next verse rules that out. James is saying that many of our battles would end if we took our desires to God instead of fighting for them. When we bring a desire to God honestly, one of three things happens: he gives it, he gives something better, or he changes the desire. All three end the war inside. What does not end the war is grabbing.

In everyday life. Underneath your last argument, at home, at work or in church, what did you want: respect, control, comfort, to be right, to be noticed? Name the desire, and bring it to God in prayer instead of fighting for it.

verseByVerse.quote: You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly, to spend it on your passions.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You ask wrongly. James anticipates the protest: “But I have asked.” The fault is the motive, not the asking.

To spend it. The verb is the one used of the prodigal son spending everything in the far country (Luke 15:14), and “passions” is the same word, pleasures, as in verse 1.

A kind refusal. These people have not abandoned prayer. They have turned it into a way of funding the very appetites that are tearing the congregation apart, and God, mercifully, declines. A father who financed every appetite his children presented would not be generous but negligent.

What would I do with it? And the verse quietly explains something that troubles many Christians. When a prayer has gone unanswered for years, the honest question is not only “Why is God silent?” but “What would I do with it if I got it?” James does not put that question to someone asking for a real need; he has just told them to ask. He puts it to our wants.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we may never pray for good things for ourselves: Jesus taught us to pray for daily bread (Matthew 6:11). We ask according to his will (1 John 5:14), not merely for our own pleasure.

How do I know whether my motives are right? Ask what you want the thing for. If God gave it, would it draw you closer to him or make you need him less? Would it serve others, or only you? Could you pray, “your will be done”, and mean it? Motives are rarely pure; most of us want good things for mixed reasons. Do not wait for perfect motives before you pray. Bring the mixture to God and ask him to purify it as you pray. Praying honestly is one of the ways he changes our motives.

I have prayed for years for something good, a child’s salvation, healing, a marriage. Are my motives wrong? Not necessarily. James is speaking about prayers to fund selfish pleasure, not about prayers for the good of others or for God’s glory. Many faithful prayers are answered slowly, or in ways we do not see, or not in this life. Abraham waited twenty-five years for Isaac. Keep praying; Jesus told a parable so that we would always pray and not lose heart (Luke 18:1). Unanswered prayer is a reason to examine your heart, yes, but also a call to trust the wisdom of a Father who knows what you do not.

For worship. When his own Son prayed, “let this cup pass from me”, the answer was no, so that every prayer of his people might be heard for his sake. The Son was refused so that we could be received. He ever lives to intercede for us (Hebrews 7:25), and he takes our muddled prayers, cleanses them, and presents them to the Father as his own.

verseByVerse.quote: You adulterous people! Do you not know that friendship with the world is enmity with God? Therefore whoever wishes to be a friend of the world makes himself an enemy of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You adulterous people! The Greek is feminine, adulteresses (moichalides), and it is not an insult about women. Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, read “adulterers and adulteresses”; the earliest have only the feminine. It is the prophets’ language, in which Israel is the bride and idolatry is infidelity (Hosea 1–3). The church is the bride of Christ (2 Corinthians 11:2). To love the world is to cheat on God. And that reframes the whole chapter: the quarrelling, the coveting and the misdirected prayers are not merely bad behaviour. They are a marriage being broken. But the God we betrayed is a husband who does not give up. When Israel played the harlot, he sent Hosea to buy back his unfaithful wife, and said, “I will betroth you to me forever” (Hosea 2:19). We are the adulteress whom Christ has redeemed and is making pure, and his faithfulness is greater than our unfaithfulness.

Do you not know that friendship with the world is enmity with God? The word for friendship carries the sense of affection and shared outlook: agreement, alliance, having the same tastes. And the world here is not the planet or the people in it, but human society organised apart from and against God, with its values of pride, greed, pleasure and self (1:27; 1 John 2:15–17). Enmity (echthra) is hostility. The claim is deliberately stark, and there is no middle category offered. James does not say friendship with the world leads to enmity, or risks it. He says it is enmity. There is no neutral ground. You cannot be friends with both.

Whoever wishes. The warning is not about living in the world or enjoying good things; the God of this letter gives every good gift (1:17). It is about where the affections are pointed: the wishing is the adultery. And “makes himself” means he does it to himself. God has not declared war on him; he has taken up a position against God. That is why the next verses can still offer him grace and not a sentence.

Enemies made friends. If friendship with the world makes a man God’s enemy, how does an enemy become a friend again? While we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son (Romans 5:10). The one who was mocked as a friend of tax collectors and sinners (Matthew 11:19) laid down his life for them, and then said to his disciples, “I have called you friends” (John 15:15). That friendship is what breaks the world’s hold, because it is better than anything the world can offer.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should hate the people of the world. God loves the world of people (John 3:16), and we are sent into it (John 17:15–18).

What counts as worldliness? Is it films, clothes, music? Worldliness is less about particular things than about the heart’s loyalty. John defines it as the desires of the flesh, the desires of the eyes and pride of life (1 John 2:16): wanting what pleases the body, what looks good, and what makes us important. A Christian can avoid every questionable film and still be thoroughly worldly in his love of money or status. Ask: where do I get my sense of worth? Whose approval do I most want? What would I be most devastated to lose? If the answer is anything other than God, that is where the world has your heart.

Can a Christian become an enemy of God? James writes to church members as a warning, and the warning is real. A professing Christian who settles into love of the world shows that his heart is drifting from God, and if he persists without repentance, he shows that his profession was never genuine (1 John 2:19). But a true believer who has strayed will be drawn back; God disciplines his children and does not let them go (Hebrews 12:6; John 10:28). The very next verses are the way back: “he gives more grace”. If you are troubled by your worldliness, that trouble is his jealous love calling you home.
verseByVerse.note: The prophets called Israel’s unfaithfulness to God “adultery.”

verseByVerse.quote: Or do you suppose it is to no purpose that the Scripture says, “He yearns jealously over the spirit that he has made to dwell in us”? But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, “God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
He yearns jealously. The plain point is not in doubt: God loves his people with a jealous love and will not share them with the world. But verse 5 is the hardest sentence in the letter to translate, and it is better to say so than to pretend to be sure. James says Scripture does not speak this in vain, yet no Old Testament text says it in these words; he seems to summarise Scripture’s teaching on God’s jealousy (Exodus 20:5; 34:14; Deuteronomy 32:16; Zechariah 8:2). There are three main readings, and the ESV margin notes the others: God yearns jealously for the human spirit he breathed into us at creation (Genesis 2:7); God yearns jealously for the Holy Spirit he made to dwell in believers; or the human spirit God made to dwell in us longs enviously, a charge against sinful desire (the KJV’s reading: “the spirit that dwelleth in us lusteth to envy”).

Whose spirit is meant? The ESV takes the first reading: God yearns jealously over the human spirit he gave us, which he wants wholly for himself. It fits the context of divided loyalty best: God will not share us with the world.

But he gives more grace. After the severity of verses 1–5, verse 6 arrives like a door opening. More grace: greater than the adultery, the quarrelling, and the appetite that has been running the congregation. Grace is favour no one has earned, given where judgment was due, and with it his power to change them (Titus 2:11–12). When we have exhausted our resolutions, he gives more. When we have betrayed him again, he gives more. God’s demand is total, but his grace is greater, enough for every failure and every temptation: “My grace is sufficient for you” (2 Corinthians 12:9).

God opposes the proud. The quotation is Proverbs 3:34 in its Greek form, and it names the one condition. Grace is not scarce, but it flows downhill, and it will not reach a man who has set himself above it. “Opposes” is a military word: to line up in battle array against. God does not merely withhold from the proud; he opposes them.

Lowly in heart. Grace collects in the low places, and the Son of God went there first. Jesus described himself with James’s own word for the humble (tapeinos): “I am gentle and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matthew 11:29). In his Son God came down to where the humble are, and his call to the weary and heavy laden is the “more grace” of verse 6, spoken in a human voice. To humble yourself is not to earn grace; it is to come to the low place where Christ is already standing.

How can God be jealous, if jealousy is a sin? Jealousy is sinful when it wants what is not ours, or resents another’s good. But there is a right jealousy, for what truly belongs to us. A husband who did not care if his wife loved another man would not be admirable. God’s jealousy is his holy, protective love for those who are his by creation and redemption. He is jealous for us, not of us; he wants our whole heart because he is our true good, and because anything else we give it to will destroy us. His name is Jealous (Exodus 34:14), and it is a name of love.

How do I become humble? Not by trying to feel small, and not by putting yourself down, which is often pride in disguise. Humility grows by looking at God: his holiness, his greatness, his grace. Isaiah saw the Lord and said, “Woe is me!” (Isaiah 6:5). It grows by looking at the cross, where we see what our sin cost and what we were given freely. And it shows itself in practice: admitting you are wrong, asking for help, serving where no one sees, rejoicing in others’ success, receiving correction without defending yourself. Humility is not thinking less of yourself; it is thinking of yourself less, because you are thinking of him.

In everyday life. Bring to mind the sin you are most ashamed of, the one you feel you have used up God’s patience on. Read these four words again: “he gives more grace”. Then do the humble thing: confess it plainly, without excuses, and receive the grace. It is not a reservoir that runs low; grace upon grace has come to us from his fullness (John 1:16).
verseByVerse.note: Verse 5 is hard to translate; the ESV margin offers other readings. No single Old Testament verse matches it; it seems to sum up Scripture’s teaching.

verseByVerse.quote: Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you. Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you. Cleanse your hands, you sinners, and purify your hearts, you double-minded.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Submit yourselves. The ten commands of verses 7–10 unpack one word from verse 6: the humble. “Submit” is military again: arrange yourself under, like soldiers under a commander. It is the opposite of the proud man’s posture, and it comes first because everything else follows from it.

Resist the devil. The order matters: submit first, then resist; a man who has not submitted to God has no ground to stand on. And the promise is not victory after a long siege but flight. The devil is real and active (1 Peter 5:8–9; Ephesians 6:11–13), but he is a defeated enemy (Hebrews 2:14).

How does a believer resist the devil? By standing firm in faith (1 Peter 5:8–9), putting on God’s armour (Ephesians 6:11–17), and answering his lies with God’s word, as Jesus did in the wilderness (Matthew 4:1–11). It does not mean shouting at Satan or using formulas; even the archangel said only, “The Lord rebuke you” (Jude 9). And the first command is “Submit yourselves therefore to God.”

Why the devil runs. The promise that he will flee is astonishing until we ask who has already fought him. Jesus met the devil in the wilderness with nothing but submission to his Father and the written word, and the devil left him (Matthew 4:11). At the cross he disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame (Colossians 2:15). The believer who submits and resists stands inside a victory already won, and the devil flees because he has already been beaten by the one the believer belongs to.

Draw near. This is priestly language, used of approaching the altar (Hebrews 7:19), and James applies it to ordinary believers. God responds to those who come to him (Zechariah 1:3; Malachi 3:7). But he is not waiting at a distance until we have travelled far enough; the chapter has just said he yearns jealously over us and gives more grace. We draw near to a God who is already leaning toward us, like the prodigal’s father, who ran (Luke 15:20). When we take one trembling step toward him, we find he has been running toward us all along, with a robe and a ring and a feast.

Cleanse your hands. Hands are outward actions; priests washed their hands before approaching God (Exodus 30:19–21). “Sinners” is a strong word for church members, used deliberately to shock.

Purify your hearts. Hands and hearts: outward conduct and inward loyalty, and both are required. “Who shall ascend the hill of the LORD?” “He who has clean hands and a pure heart” (Psalm 24:3–4). And “double-minded” is dipsychos again, the “two-souled” word of 1:8: a heart torn between God and the world. Here at last James gives its cure: not trying harder but being made clean, and the command comes only after “he gives more grace”.

Where Christians differ: does our drawing near come first, then God’s? Some read draw near to God, and he will draw near to you as teaching that human initiative comes first, and God responds; they rightly hear a real and urgent invitation in it. This commentary’s view: this command is addressed to believers already born again by God’s will (1:18), and James has just said God gives more grace (v. 6). God’s grace always comes first: no one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him (John 6:44). Within a relationship already begun by grace, God calls us to draw near and promises to meet us. Our drawing near is itself the fruit of his drawing us.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we cleanse ourselves by our own power. Christ’s blood cleanses (1 John 1:7, 9). But we must turn from sin in repentance, by grace.

I have tried to draw near, but God still feels far away. What now? Feelings are not the measure of God’s nearness. He has promised to draw near, and he keeps his promises whether you feel it or not. Many saints have walked through long seasons of spiritual dryness; the psalmists cried, “How long?” (Psalm 13:1). Keep doing what draws near: read his word, pray honestly, gather with his people, take the Lord’s Supper, confess known sin. Check for anything you are holding back from him. And rest on the fact that in Christ you have already been brought near by his blood (Ephesians 2:13). Your nearness to God rests on Christ’s work, not on your sense of it.

In everyday life. Where is the devil pressing you right now: a lie about God, an accusation, a temptation, a fear? Find one verse that answers the lie directly and say it aloud when the pressure comes.

verseByVerse.quote: Be wretched and mourn and weep. Let your laughter be turned to mourning and your joy to gloom. Humble yourselves before the Lord, and he will exalt you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Be wretched. To mourn is to grieve as for the dead; to weep is to cry aloud: deep sorrow over sin (Joel 2:12–13).

Laughter to mourning. James is addressing people who have been quarrelling, coveting and committing spiritual adultery, and doing it cheerfully. The laughter to be turned to mourning is the careless laughter of those who enjoy worldly pleasures without a thought of God (Ecclesiastes 7:2–6). Gloom is dejection, literally downcast eyes: the posture of the tax collector who would not lift up his eyes to heaven (Luke 18:13).

Godly grief. This is not a call to permanent gloom. There is a grief that is the right response to your own sin, and whoever can look at what James has just described and feel none of it has not understood. Paul calls it godly grief, and says it produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret (2 Corinthians 7:10). And if you are already low, grieving or depressed, this is not a call to pile more sorrow on yourself: James is speaking to the careless and the cheerfully worldly, and the Lord who says it is near to the brokenhearted (Psalm 34:18).

Weep now, laugh later. James is again echoing Jesus. Jesus pronounced a blessing on those who weep now, for they shall laugh, and a woe on those who laugh now, for they shall mourn and weep (Luke 6:21, 25). To turn laughter into mourning is to get onto the right side of Christ’s great reversal. The careless laughter of the world ends in tears, and the tears of repentance end in his joy, because the one who pronounced the blessing is the one who carries it out.

He will exalt you. Look at who does what. The humbling is commanded, and it is ours. The exalting is promised, and it is his. That order is the Bible’s pattern for the whole Christian life, and the exact reverse of what we do by nature: we exalt ourselves and hope God will not humble us (1 Peter 5:6). The man who goes low is not left there: James does not say humility is its own reward, but that God lifts the person who takes the low place, which is the pattern of Christ himself (Philippians 2:8–9). He mourned so that we could be comforted; he was humbled so that we could be lifted up.

How much grief is enough? I feel I can never grieve enough over my sin. Godly grief is not measured by quantity of tears, and you do not earn forgiveness by feeling bad enough. Christ’s blood, not your sorrow, pays for sin. Godly grief turns you to God; once it has done that, its work is done, and the next step is to receive forgiveness and be lifted up. If you find yourself endlessly mourning sins already confessed, that is not humility; it is failing to believe the promise (1 John 1:9). Mourn honestly, then let God exalt you. He wants his children forgiven and glad, not perpetually downcast.

Is there a place for this kind of mourning in church life today? Yes, and many churches have lost it. Times of honest confession in worship, days of prayer and humbling when a church has sinned or is in crisis, grief over a nation’s or a family’s sin: these are biblical (Nehemiah 9; Daniel 9). A church that only ever celebrates may be skipping the repentance that makes the celebration real. The joy of the gospel is deepest in people who have felt the weight of their sin.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Pride shows two more faces: the slanderer who climbs into the Judge’s seat, and the planner who takes charge of tomorrow. Both leave God out, and the section ends with a definition of sin as good known and left undone.
verseByVerse.theology:
Sin as Knowledge Not Acted On

Speaking against a brother sets us over the law instead of under it. And whoever knows the right thing to do and fails to do it, sins.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The merchants' plan was complete except for God.

Now: Plan, but hold every plan under “if the Lord wills”, life itself included.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not speak evil against one another, brothers. The one who speaks against a brother or judges his brother, speaks evil against the law and judges the law. But if you judge the law, you are not a doer of the law but a judge. There is only one lawgiver and judge, he who is able to save and to destroy. But who are you to judge your neighbor?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not speak evil. The word means to talk down, to speak against: slander, criticise, run down. It covers not only lies but any speech that tears another person down behind their back, including the accurate but damaging remark. It is the tongue of chapter 3 turned on the congregation. And the verse’s other verb, judges, means condemns, sits in judgment: setting yourself up as the judge of another’s worth or motives.

Judges the law. How does criticising a person become criticising the law? The law says love your neighbour as yourself, the royal law of 2:8, and the same paragraph of Leviticus forbids slander (Leviticus 19:16–18). If you set that aside in order to condemn somebody, you have not merely disobeyed it. You have passed judgment on it, ruling that in this case it does not apply, as if you were above it.

Not a doer but a judge. Chapter 1 divided the world into hearers and doers; here it is doers and judges. You cannot be both, because a judge stands over the law and a doer stands under it. The point of the law is to obey it, not to sit over it (1:22–25).

One lawgiver and judge. “For the LORD is our judge; the LORD is our lawgiver; the LORD is our king; he will save us” (Isaiah 33:22). God alone gives the law and judges by it. To judge others is to usurp God’s place.

Able to save and to destroy. Here is what qualifies him. Only one who can carry out the verdict either way, to save or to destroy, has the right to judge, and that describes exactly one person. Only God has power over eternal destiny (Matthew 10:28; Deuteronomy 32:39).

But who are you to judge your neighbor? The “you” is emphatic in the Greek (sy de tis ei): you, of all people? This is not bluster. It is a real question of authority: the case is not yours to try (Romans 14:4). And the last word is neighbour, which pulls Leviticus 19:18 back into the sentence one final time. The person you are judging is the person you were commanded to love.

The bench belongs to Christ. James is echoing the Lord’s warning against judging, with its speck and its log (Matthew 7:1–5). And the one Lawgiver and Judge has a name. “The Father judges no one,” Jesus said, “but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5:22), and “we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ” (2 Corinthians 5:10). The slanderer is climbing into Jesus’ seat to pass sentence on someone for whom Jesus died (Romans 14:15), someone who will stand before that seat himself and answer to his own Master, not to us.

Does this forbid all judging? No. James forbids slander and condemning a brother as if we were his final judge. Scripture still calls us to judge teaching and conduct by God’s word (1 John 4:1), and the church to exercise discipline (1 Corinthians 5:12–13). What is forbidden is taking God’s seat.

If what I say about someone is true, is it still slander? It can be. James’s word covers accurate but damaging talk behind someone’s back. Ask: why am I saying this, and to whom? If you are telling people who have no need to know, in order to lower someone in their eyes, it is sin even if every word is true. Love covers a multitude of sins (1 Peter 4:8). If the matter is serious, go to the person, or to those with responsibility to act. If it is not serious, let it go.

But what if I need to warn others about someone dangerous? That is not slander; it is love for the vulnerable. If someone is abusing, defrauding or endangering others, the truth must be spoken to those who need to know: the authorities, the elders, those at risk. Protecting the weak is commanded (Proverbs 31:8–9). Covering up harm in the name of not judging is itself a grave wrong. The difference lies in motive and audience: slander wants to damage a reputation; a warning wants to protect people. Speak the facts plainly, to the right people, and leave the final judgment of the heart to God.

In everyday life. The Judge has already borne the sentence your own words deserved, so you need not climb into his seat: this week, refuse to speak negatively about anyone behind their back. If you have a concern, go to them, or to God.

verseByVerse.quote: Come now, you who say, “Today or tomorrow we will go into such and such a town and spend a year there and trade and make a profit”— yet you do not know what tomorrow will bring. What is your life? For you are a mist that appears for a little time and then vanishes. Instead you ought to say, “If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Come now. An abrupt call to attention, and now he addresses merchants and businesspeople.

Today or tomorrow. The business plan is entirely reasonable. Timing, destination, duration, activity and outcome: all five are settled. Trade, profit and planning are not condemned; Scripture commends the ant who prepares her bread in summer (Proverbs 6:6–8). What is missing is the clause James supplies in verse 15. There is no thought of God.

You do not know. That is not gloom; it is plain fact. The plan assumes knowledge nobody has. “Do not boast about tomorrow, for you do not know what a day may bring” (Proverbs 27:1). Jesus’ parable of the rich fool makes the same point: “Fool! This night your soul is required of you” (Luke 12:16–21). Underneath the confident plan there is often a hunger for control: if I can map out tomorrow, I need not trust anyone with it, not even God. The plan becomes a refuge, and James gently takes it away so that the Lord himself can be the refuge (Psalm 46:1).

What is your life? “For you are a mist that appears for a little time and then vanishes.” The word (atmis) is used of steam, vapour or morning haze: the vapour over a field that is gone once the sun is properly up, like breath on a cold morning or steam from a pot. Not a short life. A brief appearance. Here for a moment, then gone (Job 7:7; Psalm 39:5; 102:3; 144:4). Our lives are a mist, but the Lord who holds them is not: “from everlasting to everlasting you are God” (Psalm 90:2). And because Christ gave his life for us, our mist of a life is bound up in his endless one; when the sun rises on the last day, those in him will not vanish but shine.

If the Lord wills. The correction is smaller than we expect. James does not cancel the trip or the trade. He adds a clause, and the clause covers not only the doing but the living: “If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that.” Paul used similar words (Acts 18:21). God’s providence governs all things, including our tomorrows.

Tomorrow in the Father’s hand. Behind James stands Jesus’ teaching about tomorrow. He did not cure presumption with anxiety. He told his disciples not to be anxious about tomorrow either, because their heavenly Father knows what they need, and to seek first his kingdom (Matthew 6:32–34). Boasting and worrying make the same mistake: both leave the Father out of tomorrow. “If the Lord wills” is not a shrug. It is the speech of a child who knows whose hands tomorrow is in, and it is Christ who has made us children of that Father.

Is it wrong to save, buy insurance or plan for retirement? No. Scripture commends wise preparation; Joseph stored grain for the famine, and a good man leaves an inheritance (Proverbs 13:22). The question is not whether you plan but in what spirit. Do your savings make you feel independent of God, or are they held as his, available for his purposes? Are you storing up for yourself, like the rich fool, or are you rich toward God? Plan carefully, hold the plan loosely, give generously along the way, and trust him with what you cannot control.

How do I hold my plans loosely without becoming passive or anxious? Make your plans as wisely as you can, and then pray over them, offering each one to God. When plans fail, as many will, receive it as his will rather than as a disaster. “The heart of man plans his way, but the LORD establishes his steps” (Proverbs 16:9). This is not fatalism; it is trust. It frees you from the anxiety of having to control tomorrow, and from the pride of thinking you can. You do your part today, and leave tomorrow to the one who holds it.

verseByVerse.quote: As it is, you boast in your arrogance. All such boasting is evil. So whoever knows the right thing to do and fails to do it, for him it is sin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You boast in your arrogance. The word for arrogance comes from the Greek figure of the braggart, often pictured as the travelling impostor who claimed powers he did not have. They boast about their plans as if the future were theirs to command: the pride of life (1 John 2:16).

All such boasting is evil. Not unwise, not naive. Evil, because it is a claim to a knowledge and a control that belong to God alone, made by a mist. It is practical atheism: living as though God did not rule.

Whoever knows the right thing. Verse 17 reads like a detached proverb, but the “So” ties it to what goes before. These men now know about the mist and the “If the Lord wills”, so their planning can no longer be excused as thoughtlessness.

Sin as omission. We usually think of sin as doing what is forbidden. James adds that it is also sin not to do what we know is right. That is a sin of omission: good left undone.

The whole letter in a sentence. Verse 17 compresses the letter. The man who hears and does not do is deceiving himself (1:22); the man who says and does not give is useless (2:16); the man who knows and does not act is sinning. James never charges his readers with not knowing, only with knowing and not doing. That is sobering for anyone who hears much and reads much: we answer for more with every sermon understood and every chapter agreed with (Luke 12:47).

Not done to me. Jesus taught the same truth in the starkest terms. In his picture of the last judgment, those on the King’s left are not condemned for crimes they committed but for the hungry they did not feed and the prisoners they did not visit, and the King says that what they did not do for the least of these, they did not do for him (Matthew 25:41–46). Sins of omission are never mere gaps. The good left undone was good owed to Christ, in the person he set in our path.

There is so much good I could do. Am I sinning all the time by not doing it? No. James is not saying you must do every good thing in the world, which no one can. He means the specific good that God puts in front of you and that you know you ought to do: the call you should make, the apology you owe, the need right in front of you, the duty of your own calling. God gives each of us particular responsibilities and limits; even Jesus did not heal everyone in Israel. Ask: what has God clearly put in my path? Do that, and trust him with the rest. This verse should lead to obedience, not to paralysis.

What about the good I failed to do in the past? Bring it to Christ. Sins of omission are forgiven like any other sin through his blood (1 John 1:9). Where you can still put something right, do it; where you cannot, leave it with him. Then let this verse shape tomorrow rather than haunt yesterday. The purpose of the warning is not to load you with guilt but to move you to act now, while it is still today.

In everyday life. What good thing do you know you should do but have been putting off? Do it today, in the strength of the Spirit who now lives in you; if it is too big for today, take the first step today.

For worship. Only one man never failed to do the good he knew. Jesus always knew his Father’s will, and he did all of it: “I always do the things that are pleasing to him” (John 8:29). And he bore our sins of omission as well as our sins of commission, the good we left undone along with the evil we did, and his perfect doing is counted as ours. He did not boast about tomorrow; he gave himself for our tomorrows, and rose to make them his.
