5.title: Patient Until He Comes: Wealth, Endurance, and Prayer
5.overview:
The last chapter moves from prophetic warning to pastoral tenderness. It opens with the letter’s most severe passage (vv. 1–6), a woe against rich oppressors who withheld wages and lived in luxury while the righteous suffered.

Then James turns gently to the suffering church (vv. 7–20): patience because the Lord is coming, prayer in every condition, and, at the very end, a wanderer brought home.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: James speaks to the rich oppressors as the prophets spoke to the nations, while the church overhears: their hoarded wealth is already decaying, and the cheated harvesters have been heard by the Lord of hosts.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Rust That Testifies

Hoarded wealth will testify against those who kept back the wages of their labourers. The cries of the harvesters have reached the Lord of hosts.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A day-labourer's withheld wage meant a family without supper.

Now: Comfort bought by someone else's hunger is not a blessing but fattening for a day of slaughter.

verseByVerse.quote: Come now, you rich, weep and howl for the miseries that are coming upon you. Your riches have rotted and your garments are moth-eaten. Your gold and silver have corroded, and their corrosion will be evidence against you and will eat your flesh like fire. You have laid up treasure in the last days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. James closes with the rich oppressors denounced (vv. 1–6), patient endurance as the Lord’s coming draws near (vv. 7–12), prayer in every condition (vv. 13–18), and a wanderer brought home (vv. 19–20). Over it all stands the coming Lord, compassionate and merciful, who hears the cries of harvesters and the prayers of ordinary people.

Come now, you rich. The same abrupt summons as in 4:13. The rich are probably wealthy unbelievers who oppressed the poor believers (2:6–7). As the prophets addressed the nations while God’s people listened (Isaiah 13; Amos 4:1), James addresses the oppressors, and the believers overhear and are comforted that God sees.

Weep and howl. The verb is violent, the shriek of open grief, used of those under God’s judgment (Isaiah 13:6; 15:3). The miseries “are coming”: they are still future, but certain, and James tells the rich to weep now because of them.

Your riches have rotted. Three kinds of wealth, each longer-lasting than the one before: food, clothing, metal. All three have failed. Rot is what happens to grain and produce, stored wealth that could spoil, like the rich fool’s barns (Luke 12:18–20).

Moth-eaten garments. Fine clothing was stored wealth in that world, a major form of savings, and it takes no thief to lose it: a moth will do. “Do not lay up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy” (Matthew 6:19–20).

Gold and silver corroded. Gold does not corrode, and James knows it. He is making a point by overstatement: the one asset that cannot decay has decayed. Nothing they own has survived.

Evidence against you. The word is a legal term: testimony for the prosecution. Metal that is spent does not corrode; this corroded because it was hoarded while the men who earned it went hungry.

Eat your flesh like fire. The corrosion that consumed the treasure will consume the owner: the wealth they trusted becomes the instrument of their judgment.

In the last days. The last days are the final age before judgment, which began with Christ (Acts 2:17; Hebrews 1:2). They were piling up wealth just when it could do them least good, like a man buying property in a town he knows is to be flooded.

Treasure in heaven. James sharpens Jesus’ own woe to the rich (Luke 6:24). But Jesus did not only warn. When a rich man asked about eternal life, Jesus looked at him, loved him, and offered him treasure in heaven if he would give to the poor and follow him (Mark 10:21). The hoarders of verse 3 were storing up the one kind of treasure that perishes, in the very age when the other kind was being offered. The Judge who will call the hoarders to account is the one who emptied himself of every treasure: “though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor” (2 Corinthians 8:9). He had nowhere to lay his head, and he was buried in a borrowed tomb. He is our treasure, and he does not rust.

What it does not mean. It does not mean all wealth is evil: Abraham, Job and Joseph of Arimathea were rich and godly. James condemns hoarding, oppression, fraud and self-indulgence.

If I am comfortably off, is this passage about me? Its first target is the unbelieving rich who exploited the church, but it searches anyone with more than they need, which includes most readers in the West. The questions it asks are not how much you have, but how you got it, whether you are hoarding it, and whether anyone has gone without because of you. Paul gives the positive command: the rich are to do good, to be rich in good works, generous and ready to share, so storing up treasure as a good foundation for the future (1 Timothy 6:17–19). Wealth held open-handed is a tool for the kingdom. Wealth clutched is a witness for the prosecution.

How do I know if I am hoarding rather than saving wisely? Saving for real needs, a home, your children, old age, emergencies, is wise and biblical (Proverbs 6:6–8; 1 Timothy 5:8). Hoarding is keeping far beyond need out of fear or love of money, while needs around you go unmet. Some honest tests: Do I give generously and regularly, or only from what is left over? Does my security rest in my savings or in God? If God asked me to give a large part away, would I feel grief or freedom? Is there a need in front of me that I could meet and am refusing to? Talk it through with a wise believer; money is the area where we deceive ourselves most easily.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, the wages of the laborers who mowed your fields, which you kept back by fraud, are crying out against you, and the cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord of hosts. You have lived on the earth in luxury and in self-indulgence. You have fattened your hearts in a day of slaughter. You have condemned and murdered the righteous person. He does not resist you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wages kept back by fraud. The law was explicit: a hired man was to be paid before sunset, because he is poor and counts on it (Leviticus 19:13; Deuteronomy 24:14–15). A day-labourer had no savings; to withhold his wage overnight was not a cashflow decision. It was a family going without supper.

Crying out. There are two cries: the wages themselves cry, and so do the men, as Abel’s blood cried to God from the ground (Genesis 4:10).

The Lord of hosts. This is the military title: the LORD of armies, who defends the oppressed (Isaiah 5:9). The defrauded workers have no advocate, no court and no standing, and yet their case has been heard by the commander of heaven’s armies, who said at the burning bush that he had heard his people’s cry (Exodus 3:7).

Good news to the poor. The Lord of hosts who hears the harvesters did more than hear. In Jesus he came among working people, known in Nazareth as the carpenter (Mark 6:3), and his first sermon announced good news to the poor and liberty for the oppressed (Luke 4:18). The defrauded worker has an advocate who once worked with his own hands.

Luxury and self-indulgence. Soft living and wanton pleasure, like the rich man who feasted every day while Lazarus lay at his gate (Luke 16:19). This luxury was funded by that unpaid wage: comfort at one table bought by hunger at another.

A day of slaughter. Like cattle fattened for the slaughter (Jeremiah 12:3), they have stuffed themselves, not knowing what the day is for. They took their prosperity as a sign of God’s favour; James says it was fattening them for judgment.

Condemned and murdered. “Condemned” is a courtroom word: the courts were used against a man who could not afford to defend himself (2:6), which for a day-labourer could mean death. “The righteous person” means the innocent poor in general, and perhaps also points to Jesus, the Righteous One (Acts 3:14; 7:52).

He does not resist you. There was never a contest: the righteous poor are helpless, or choose not to retaliate (Matthew 5:39). Some take it as a question: “Does not God oppose you?” (as in 4:6). Either way, the powerless man’s silence is not the end of the matter. And the Righteous One did not resist those who condemned him. He stood silent before a rigged court, was condemned by the powerful, and in his silence he bore the sins of oppressors and oppressed alike. His blood cries out like Abel’s, but it speaks a better word than the blood of Abel (Hebrews 12:24): not vengeance, but forgiveness for all who come to him.

What does this mean for me as an employer, a customer or a manager? If you employ or pay anyone, pay them fairly and on time, and do not use your power to squeeze those who cannot push back. That includes the cleaner, the builder, the freelancer whose invoice sits unpaid for months. “Masters, treat your bondservants justly and fairly, knowing that you also have a Master in heaven” (Colossians 4:1). As a customer, it is worth asking, as far as you reasonably can, whether the cheapness of what you buy depends on someone else’s exploitation. No one can know everything, but a Christian should care, and act where he can.

Is God on the side of the poor? God is on the side of justice, and Scripture repeatedly shows him as the defender of the poor, the widow and the oppressed, who hears their cry when no one else does (Psalm 146:7–9). But that does not mean the poor are saved by being poor, or the rich condemned by being rich; salvation is by grace through faith in Christ for all. What it means is that the oppressed have a Judge, and oppressors will answer to him. The church should share his heart: speaking up for the voiceless, and refusing to flatter the powerful.

If God hears the cry, why does he let the cheating go on so long? The psalmist asked exactly that, and it troubled him until he went into the sanctuary of God and saw their end (Psalm 73:16–17). James gives the same answer: the cries have already reached the Lord’s ears, and the account is being kept, down to the last unpaid wage. The delay is not deafness. The Lord is not slow to fulfil his promise but patient, not wishing that any should perish, the oppressor included (2 Peter 3:9). So the wronged can wait without despair, and the wrongdoer still has time to repent and repay, as Zacchaeus did (Luke 19:8).

In everyday life. Check this week whether there is any bill, wage or debt you have been sitting on, and pay it. If you are the one defrauded, bring your cry to the Lord of hosts, plainly and in detail.
verseByVerse.note: The Law required day-labourers to be paid the same day.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–20 — Patience, Prayer, and Going After the Wanderer
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: James turns back to the suffering church. Because the Lord is coming, they can wait without revenge or grumbling, and pray in trouble, in gladness and in sickness, as ordinary people whose prayers God hears.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Prayer of Faith

Be patient as the farmer waits for the rains, because the Lord is coming. Pray in every condition; the prayer of faith is prayer submitted to God's will, and Elijah was a man like us.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Pressed from outside, the congregation was grumbling against one another.

Now: The letter ends by sending ordinary believers after the one who has wandered.

verseByVerse.quote: Be patient, therefore, brothers, until the coming of the Lord. See how the farmer waits for the precious fruit of the earth, being patient about it, until it receives the early and the late rains. You also, be patient. Establish your hearts, for the coming of the Lord is at hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Be patient, therefore. James turns back to the congregation, and his tone softens. “Therefore” means: because God will judge the oppressors. The word for patience (makrothymia) means long-tempered, slow to burn: the patience that does not hit back. Having heard their oppressors denounced, they might take matters into their own hands. James says: wait.

The coming of the Lord. The word (parousia) was used of a king’s official visit (1 Thessalonians 4:15). They are not waiting for nothing; they are waiting for someone else to act, and on that day all wrongs will be put right.

The farmer waits. In Israel the early rain came in autumn and the late rain in spring (Deuteronomy 11:14; Joel 2:23), with months between them in which nothing could be done. The farmer has ploughed and sown, and he will reap, but no activity in the world brings the harvest forward by a day. It is certain, and it comes at its proper time.

Establish your hearts. To establish is to make firm. To wait well, the heart must be made steady, and it is God who establishes us in Christ, with his Spirit in our hearts as a guarantee (2 Corinthians 1:21–22).

At hand. The Greek means he has drawn near and is near now (Romans 13:11–12; Philippians 4:5). James gives no date, but the nearness turns patience into hope.

Where Christians differ: was James wrong about the nearness of Christ’s return? Critics argue that the early church expected Jesus to return within their lifetime and was mistaken. This commentary’s view: near in the New Testament describes the character of the whole age since Christ’s resurrection. Christ’s return is the next great event in God’s plan, and it is near: no date is given, and every generation must live ready (James 5:8; Revelation 22:7). Paul also says that a final rebellion and the man of lawlessness will come first (2 Thessalonians 2:3), so near does not mean that no prophecy remains; but these things are not a timetable to calculate, for the mystery of lawlessness is already at work (2 Thessalonians 2:7), and the day will still come like a thief on those who are not watching (1 Thessalonians 5:2–4). God’s timetable is not ours; with the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day (2 Peter 3:8–9). The delay is God’s patience, giving time for repentance. Christ will come once, visibly and gloriously, to judge and to renew all things.

Was James wrong, since two thousand years have passed? At hand means that Christ’s coming is the next great event in God’s plan and could come in any generation, with no date that anyone may count on, not that it would come within a few years. Peter answers the same objection: with the Lord one day is as a thousand years, and his delay is patience, giving time for repentance (2 Peter 3:8–9).

What will actually happen when he comes? Scripture describes one visible, glorious return of Christ at the end of this age, seen by all (Acts 1:11; Revelation 1:7). There is no secret coming beforehand. Many Christians have been taught to expect a secret rapture of the church before a time of tribulation, and they hold it out of real love for his appearing; this commentary reads the passages differently, because the coming in 1 Thessalonians 4 is loud and public, with a cry of command and the trumpet of God, and the New Testament speaks of one return, not two. At his coming the dead will be raised, believers who are alive will be changed and caught up to meet him, and he will judge the living and the dead (1 Thessalonians 4:16–17; 1 Corinthians 15:51–52; Matthew 25:31–46). The wicked will go away into eternal punishment, and the righteous into eternal life; and God will make all things new, a new heaven and a new earth in which righteousness dwells (2 Peter 3:13). That is the harvest the farmer waits for.

If I am suffering injustice now, does patience mean I should not seek justice? No. Patience forbids revenge and bitterness, not lawful justice. Paul appealed to Caesar and insisted on his rights as a Roman citizen (Acts 16:37; 25:11). If you are wronged, you may use proper means: the courts, the police, the employment tribunal, the church’s elders. If you are being abused, get to safety and report it. What James forbids is taking vengeance into your own hands, and the despair that thinks God has forgotten. Pursue justice by right means, and leave the final reckoning to the Lord, who will repay (Romans 12:19).

For worship. The one who came first in weakness, to a manger and a cross, will come again in glory, and every eye will see him. He will judge every wrong, comfort every mourner, and raise his people from the dust. The farmer’s waiting ends in harvest, and the harvest is Christ himself and all who belong to him. “Amen. Come, Lord Jesus!” (Revelation 22:20).
verseByVerse.note: In Israel the early rain came in autumn, at sowing, and the late rain in spring, before harvest.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not grumble against one another, brothers, so that you may not be judged; behold, the Judge is standing at the door.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not grumble. The word means to groan or sigh: not open quarrelling but muttering, the remark to one person about another, like Israel grumbling in the wilderness (1 Corinthians 10:10).

Pressure goes sideways. James puts this warning here for a reason. When people are pressed from outside and cannot push back, they take it out on those nearest to them, as in families under financial strain and teams under a difficult boss.

So that you may not be judged. To grumble about someone is to pass sentence on him in private (4:11–12), and the man who sets himself up as judge will be judged himself (Matthew 7:1).

The Judge is standing at the door. The Judge is Christ (Acts 10:42), about to enter (Matthew 24:33). It is a comfort: the oppressed are told their Judge has arrived at the building. And it is a warning in the same breath: he is at the door of their room too, about to walk in on the muttering.

What is the difference between grumbling and lament? Lament takes the complaint to God; grumbling takes it to everyone except God, and except the person concerned. Lament is honest about pain and ends in trust: “How long, O LORD?” but “I have trusted in your steadfast love” (Psalm 13:1, 5). Grumbling is resentful and goes round in circles. Lament seeks God’s help; grumbling seeks allies. If you have a real grievance against a brother, go to him (Matthew 18:15). If you have a grief you cannot fix, take it to God. Either way, stop muttering.

For worship. The Judge at the door is the Saviour who knocks: if anyone opens the door, “I will come in to him and eat with him” (Revelation 3:20). He bore with the grumbling of Israel for forty years, and of his disciples through his ministry. His patience with us is the reason we can be patient with one another.

verseByVerse.quote: As an example of suffering and patience, brothers, take the prophets who spoke in the name of the Lord. Behold, we consider those blessed who remained steadfast. You have heard of the steadfastness of Job, and you have seen the purpose of the Lord, how the Lord is compassionate and merciful.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Take the prophets. The prophets, like Jeremiah, Elijah and Isaiah, suffered rejection, imprisonment and death (Matthew 5:12; Hebrews 11:32–38), not despite their faithfulness but because they spoke in the Lord’s name. James is telling a congregation oppressed for their faith that they stand in the prophets’ line, not outside it.

Those blessed who remained steadfast. Here James goes back to hypomonē, the steadfast endurance of chapter 1, and “blessed” repeats 1:12. The letter ends where it began.

The steadfastness of Job. Job was not patient in the sense the word has acquired in English. He protested at length and told God he had a case to argue. What he did was not let go of God (Job 1:21), which is what hypomonē means: “Though he slay me, I will hope in him” (Job 13:15); “I know that my Redeemer lives” (Job 19:25). Endurance is not silence but holding on.

The purpose of the Lord. The word (telos) means the end, the outcome: how it turned out. God restored Job and revealed himself to him (Job 42:10–17). Job could not see it from inside; the reader of the book can, and that is the advantage James is handing them.

Compassionate and merciful. A remarkable conclusion from a book that never explains Job’s suffering. James does not say the Lord explained himself; he says the end of the story showed what he was like, echoing God’s self-description at Sinai: “a God merciful and gracious” (Exodus 34:6). What the Lord brought about at the end of Job’s story is a glimpse; what he brought about in history is a cross and an empty tomb. There we see how compassionate and merciful he is.

Compassion with a face. James’s rare word (polysplanchnos) is built on the word for the inward parts, and the Gospels use its verb again and again of Jesus: when he saw the crowds harassed and helpless, and the widow of Nain behind her son’s bier, he had compassion (Matthew 9:36; Luke 7:13). What Job glimpsed at the end of his book, the reader of the Gospels can watch walking through Galilee.

Is it all right to complain to God the way Job did? Yes, if you complain to him and not away from him. The book of Psalms is full of honest complaint, and God included it in Scripture to teach us how to pray in the dark. Job’s friends, who defended God with tidy explanations, were rebuked; Job, who wrestled honestly, was vindicated (Job 42:7). What God did correct in Job was the edge of accusation, the demand that God answer to him (Job 38–40). So pour out your heart, ask your questions, and then, like Job, put your hand over your mouth before his majesty and keep trusting.

Will God give me back what I lost, as he did for Job? He may, in this life, in some measure; he often does restore. But he has not promised that every loss will be repaid here. The deeper promise is that nothing is finally lost for those in Christ. The children Job buried were not replaced by the new ones, but Job looked for a Redeemer who would stand on the earth at the last. Our end, our telos, is resurrection, reunion, and a world made new. The compassion of the Lord will be seen fully not at the end of a chapter but at the end of the story.

In everyday life. If someone you know is suffering, do not be Job’s friends. Sit with them, listen, weep with them, and resist the urge to explain.

verseByVerse.quote: But above all, my brothers, do not swear, either by heaven or by earth or by any other oath, but let your “yes” be yes and your “no” be no, so that you may not fall under condemnation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Above all, do not swear. “Above all” most likely marks a final, weighty point. It may come here because people under suffering make rash oaths. It echoes Jesus almost word for word (Matthew 5:33–37).

By heaven or by earth. James has in view the habit of propping up ordinary speech with oaths: swearing by heaven, by earth, by the temple. A graded system grew up in which some oaths bound and others were escape routes (Matthew 23:16–22). Jesus and James reject the game: all speech is spoken before God. A man who must swear to be believed has admitted that his ordinary word is not reliable.

Truly, I say to you. Jesus never swore by heaven or by the temple. He began his weightiest sayings with “Truly, I say to you” (in his own language, “Amen”), and no oath propped them up, because he is the truth (John 14:6). The plain yes James asks of us is learned from him.

Under condemnation. The warning sounds heavier than the subject deserves, and that is the point. A graded oath system is a device for deceiving while appearing truthful, and God is not deceived by the gradations.

Where Christians differ: are all oaths forbidden? Some groups, such as Quakers and Anabaptists, refuse to take any oath, including in court, out of a sincere wish to obey Jesus’ words to the letter. This commentary’s view: James and Jesus forbid casual, frivolous, evasive oaths in everyday speech, and the habit of using oaths to manipulate. They do not forbid solemn, lawful oaths when required by proper authority, as in court. God himself swore oaths (Hebrews 6:13–18); Jesus answered under oath before the high priest (Matthew 26:63–64); Paul called God as witness (Romans 1:9; 2 Corinthians 1:23). The Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession rightly regard lawful oaths as part of religious worship (Westminster 22.1; 1689 23.1). The heart of the command is simple, consistent truthfulness.

Does this forbid all oaths, even in court or at a wedding? Quakers and many Anabaptists have held that it does. But God himself swears by himself (Hebrews 6:13–17), Paul calls God as witness (Romans 1:9; 2 Corinthians 1:23), and Jesus answered when put under oath (Matthew 26:63–64). The Reformed confessions therefore allow solemn and lawful oaths. What James forbids is casual swearing, oaths used to make some words binding and others not. A Christian’s plain word should be enough. Wedding vows and the solemn promises of church membership or ordination are lawful vows made before God, and should be kept.

What about phrases like I swear, honestly, or to be honest with you? They are the modern version of the same habit, and worth noticing in your own speech. If you need to say honestly, what does that imply about the rest of what you say? Most of these are thoughtless habits rather than wicked oaths, but James invites us to drop the props and let our plain words carry the weight. The same goes for exaggeration: always, never, literally, everyone. Truthful people speak plainly, and their plain speech is trusted.

In everyday life. Every promise of God is Yes in Christ, and his truthfulness is counted as yours even where your word has failed. Keep every promise you make this week, including the small ones; if you cannot keep one, say so honestly and early.

verseByVerse.quote: Is anyone among you suffering? Let him pray. Is anyone cheerful? Let him sing praise.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Is anyone among you suffering? “Let him pray.” Three questions in quick succession, the first two with a one-word answer in the Greek, and together they turn every mood of the Christian life into prayer or praise. Suffering (kakopathei) covers hardship and misfortune of any kind; it has the same root as the suffering of the prophets in verse 10. And the response is not resignation or despair, not grumbling (v. 9) or swearing (v. 12), and not a search for the reason. Pray (proseuchesthō, keep praying).

In the flow. The patience of verses 7–11 prays while it waits, and the letter comes full circle: it opened with trials and asking God in faith (1:2–8), and closes with sickness and the prayer of faith (5:15).

Is anyone cheerful? “Let him sing praise.” And that is the half we habitually neglect. Cheerful (euthymei) is in good spirits, happy; sing praise (psalletō) is to sing psalms, sing with music (Ephesians 5:19; Colossians 3:16). Most Christians know that trouble should send them to God; far fewer see that gladness should send them to him too.

Every day goes up. Trouble goes up as prayer, joy goes up as song, and between them they cover every day anybody has. A man who prays only when suffering has a relationship with his own need rather than with God. James is not against any emotion; he is against every emotion being kept to oneself.

Through one name. Both the groan and the song go up by the same way: we ask the Father in Jesus’ name (John 16:23–24). So the sufferer does not have to compose himself before he prays, and the glad man does not have to justify his gladness; both come in the name of the Son.

What if I am neither suffering nor cheerful, just flat and numb? Then bring the numbness. The Psalms include prayers from people who felt nothing but distance (Psalm 88). Read a psalm aloud and let its words carry you when your own are gone. Keep the habits of prayer and worship going even when they feel mechanical; they are like keeping a fire laid, ready to catch. Tell God plainly that you feel nothing. And if the flatness persists for a long time, talk to someone; it may be depression, which needs care, not condemnation.

I cannot sing well. Does that matter? Not at all. God is not listening for quality but for hearts. Singing in Scripture is commanded for all God’s people, not just the musical (Psalm 100:1–2), and the joyful noise counts. Sing in the car, hum while you work, read a psalm of praise aloud if singing is impossible. The point is that joy is directed to God rather than kept to yourself.

For worship. The Son himself prayed with loud cries and tears (Hebrews 5:7), and sang a hymn with his disciples on the night he was betrayed (Matthew 26:30). He has gone before us into every human condition, and now he leads the praise of his people: “in the midst of the congregation I will sing your praise” (Hebrews 2:12). Whether we weep or laugh, we never come to God alone.

verseByVerse.quote: Is anyone among you sick? Let him call for the elders of the church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord. And the prayer of faith will save the one who is sick, and the Lord will raise him up. And if he has committed sins, he will be forgiven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Is anyone among you sick? “Let him call for the elders of the church.” Sick (asthenei) is weak, ill, probably seriously ill, since the elders come to him rather than him going to them. The sick man is the one who calls (proskalesasthō, summon). And the word is plural (presbyterous): he calls the elders, the ordinary appointed leaders of the local congregation. Prayer for the sick is not left to individuals with special gifts; it is part of the elders’ ordinary pastoral care.

Anointing him with oil. They pray over him, and the anointing is subordinate to the praying. Oil was both medicine (Luke 10:34) and a sign of setting someone apart for God (1 Samuel 16:13); the Twelve also anointed the sick (Mark 6:13). Whether the oil is chiefly medicine or sign, it is not what matters most. The praying is, and it is done in the name of the Lord.

The prayer of faith. The power is not in the oil or the elders but in God. Save means rescue, heal, restore: here primarily physical healing, though it can include more.

The Lord at the bedside. In the Gospels the sick were carried to Jesus, and he healed them with a word or a touch (Mark 1:32–34). He is ascended now, but he is not a different Lord. The elders bring the sick man to him in prayer, and his compassion has not cooled (Hebrews 13:8), even when his answer is not the one we asked for.

Handled honestly. Read on its own, this seems to promise that every believing prayer heals, and every Christian knows it does not. Asking can be answered no (4:3), and Paul was not always healed or able to heal (2 Timothy 4:20). The prayer of faith is not prayer with enough confidence worked up: that would make the sick man’s illness his own fault, the very cruelty this verse has often been used to inflict. It is prayer offered in submission to God’s will. And “save” and “raise up” reach beyond recovery: every believer will finally be raised up at the resurrection, whether or not this illness ends.

If he has committed sins. The “if” is careful and merciful. Not all sickness is caused by sin (John 9:2–3), but some is (1 Corinthians 11:30). If sin is involved, confession and prayer bring forgiveness. James allows that sin may be involved and refuses to assume it, which is exactly the balance Job’s friends failed to keep.

Where Christians differ: is this a sacrament of last rites, or a promise of guaranteed healing? Roman Catholic teaching sees this as the sacrament of the anointing of the sick (formerly extreme unction, given to the dying). Some teachers in the healing and prosperity movements take it as a guarantee that God always heals in response to faith. This commentary’s view: James describes prayer for the sick aimed at recovery, not preparation for death, so it is not last rites; and Scripture names only two sacraments, or ordinances, that Christ commanded his church to keep: baptism and the Lord’s Supper. Nor is it an unconditional guarantee: God answers according to his will (1 John 5:14), and even Paul left Trophimus ill (2 Timothy 4:20) and was not healed of his thorn (2 Corinthians 12:7–9). This passage gives a continuing pattern for church life: elders praying with faith for the sick, using oil as a sign if they choose, trusting God to heal as he wills. This is distinct from the apostolic sign gifts of healing, which have ceased; God still heals in answer to prayer. This commentary holds that those gifts were signs confirming the apostles’ message while the New Testament was being given (Acts 2:43; 2 Corinthians 12:12; Hebrews 2:3–4), and it is telling that James sends the sick man to the elders, not to a healer. Many faithful Christians, including Pentecostal and charismatic brothers and sisters, believe such gifts continue today and pray for the sick with real love and faith; we differ with them as brothers, and on both views the sick are brought to the same compassionate Lord.

Is this the basis for the Roman Catholic sacrament of the anointing of the sick? It was once given mainly to the dying as last rites. But James speaks of anointing the sick to pray for their recovery, “the Lord will raise him up”, not to prepare them for death, and the healing comes from the prayer and the Lord, not from a sacrament.

Should churches still anoint with oil? The oil was used in the ancient world both as medicine and as a sign of setting someone apart for God; here, with prayer in the Lord’s name, it is most likely a sign. Elders may still pray over the sick and anoint them, and this does not oppose medicine; Christians should use doctors and pray. God often heals, but not always; Paul left Trophimus ill (2 Timothy 4:20).

We prayed, and my loved one died. Was our faith too weak? No. Hear this clearly: the death of someone you prayed for is not proof that you lacked faith or that God did not hear. Faith is not a force that obliges God; it is trust in his wisdom and love, and sometimes his answer is to take his child home. For the believer, death is the final healing: the Lord raised them up, not from the sickbed but into his presence, where there is no more pain (Revelation 21:4). Your prayers were not wasted; they were part of carrying your loved one to the Lord. Grieve freely, as one who has hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13), and do not let anyone load you with guilt this verse never imposed.

How do I actually call for the elders? Simply ask. Contact your pastor or one of the elders, explain that you are seriously ill, and ask them to come and pray with you, as James says. They may come to your home or the hospital, read Scripture, ask whether there is anything you want to confess, pray for healing and for God’s will, and perhaps anoint you with a little oil on the forehead. It is not a ritual to be performed correctly but an act of the church’s care. Many believers never ask because they do not want to be a bother. James says: call them.
verseByVerse.note: Oil was used as medicine and as a sign of setting someone apart for God.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed. The prayer of a righteous person has great power as it is working.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Confess your sins to one another. Since sin may sometimes lie behind trouble, deal with it in the open. James does not mean confession to a priest, nor to God only, but ordinary Christians telling each other the truth about themselves. It needs no special office, and most of us avoid it.

Why it works. Sin kept private grows in the dark and is fed by the fear of exposure; once a man has told somebody, the secrecy that protected the sin is gone. “When I kept silent, my bones wasted away” (Psalm 32:3–5).

Confessed under the cross. Confession between believers is safe only because Christ carried our sins to the cross: “By his wounds you have been healed,” Peter says, using James’s word for healing (1 Peter 2:24). So the brother who hears a confession does not absolve and need not be shocked; he points to a sin already carried, and prays. For those in Christ there is no condemnation (Romans 8:1). The darkness where sin hid is flooded with his light, and the light does not condemn.

Pray for one another. Confession alone leaves a person exposed, so James joins it to intercession, for healing of body, soul and community (Hebrews 12:13).

Great power as it is working. The last phrase is difficult and probably means “in its working”: prayer is not power kept in store but power at work, effective as it is being prayed. God works powerfully through the prayers of ordinary believers.

Righteous is not a rare class. Righteous does not mean a sinless super-saint, or the verse would discourage the very people it was written for. It means a believer whose sins are confessed and forgiven, and James’s example, Elijah, was made of the same stuff as we are.

Where Christians differ: is confession to a priest required? Roman Catholic teaching requires confession of serious sins to a priest for absolution. This commentary’s view: James commands mutual confession to one another, among all believers, not confession to a priestly class. Forgiveness comes from God through Christ, our only mediator (1 Timothy 2:5; 1 John 1:9). Confessing sins to a trusted fellow believer or elder is a valuable means of grace, accountability and healing, but it is not a sacrament, and no human being stands between the believer and God.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every sin must be confessed publicly to the whole church. Wisdom guides what to confess and to whom: a sin against a person to that person; private struggles to a trusted friend or elder.

Whom should I confess to, and how? Choose a mature, trustworthy believer of the same sex, or an elder, someone who will keep confidence, point you to Christ, pray for you and help you fight. Be specific rather than vague; “I have been struggling” is not confession. Say what you did. Then ask them to pray, there and then if possible, and to ask you about it again. If you have sinned against someone, confess to that person and seek to make it right. And remember that you are confessing to a fellow sinner, not to a judge: the one you tell also needs grace.

What if the person I confess to betrays my trust? That is a real risk, and it is why you should choose carefully. A believer who gossips about a confession has sinned seriously and should be lovingly confronted. But do not let the fear of that stop you entirely; most Christians, when trusted with a confession, are humbled and honoured, and keep it. Start small, with someone you have good reason to trust, and let the friendship grow. And if a confession involves a crime, particularly harm to a child or vulnerable person, it must not be kept secret; protecting the vulnerable comes before confidentiality.

In everyday life. Be the kind of person others can confess to: unshockable, discreet, quick to pray and quick to point to Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Elijah was a man with a nature like ours, and he prayed fervently that it might not rain, and for three years and six months it did not rain on the earth. Then he prayed again, and heaven gave rain, and the earth bore its fruit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A nature like ours. Elijah is among the most spectacular prophets: fire from heaven on Carmel, ravens that fed him, a chariot of fire. He is exactly the man a discouraged congregation would point to as proof that prayer works for other people. James removes the objection at once: Elijah had the same nature as we have.

Not immune to despair. Right after one of the most dramatic answers to prayer in the Old Testament, he sat under a broom tree and asked God to let him die (1 Kings 19:3–4). The God who answered a depressed prophet under that broom tree, sending an angel with bread and water and then a low whisper, is the same God who hears us.

He prayed fervently. Literally “he prayed with prayer”, a Hebrew idiom for earnestness. 1 Kings 17:1 records his announcement of the drought; James understands it to have rested on prayer. The drought was God’s judgment on Ahab’s idolatry (Deuteronomy 11:16–17).

Three years and six months. The Lord gives the same figure (Luke 4:25), though 1 Kings 18:1 says the word came in the third year, probably counting from Elijah’s stay at Zarephath, so that the whole drought lasted about three and a half years.

He prayed again. On Carmel Elijah bowed with his face between his knees, sent his servant to look seven times, and rain came (1 Kings 18:41–45). The closing image returns to the farmer of verse 7 waiting for the rains.

The righteous man who is always heard. The Son of God also took a nature like ours (Hebrews 2:17), and at Lazarus’s tomb he said he knew the Father always hears him (John 11:41–42). He always lives to intercede for his people (Hebrews 7:25). So the prayers of weak believers, despairing under their own broom trees, are joined to the intercession of a righteous man who is never refused.

Can I pray for things like rain, or a job, or a parking space? Yes. Nothing that concerns you is too small to bring to your Father, who numbers the hairs of your head (Matthew 10:30). Elijah prayed about the weather because it mattered to God’s purposes and to his people. Pray about everything, and hold every request with an open hand: “your will be done”. The difference between Elijah’s prayer and a superstitious one is not the size of the request but its submission. He prayed in line with what God had said, and he prayed for God’s name to be honoured.

What does fervent prayer look like for an ordinary person? Not necessarily long or loud, but earnest and persistent. Elijah sent his servant to look seven times. Fervent prayer means praying as though it matters, because it does: specific requests rather than vague wishes, prayer that keeps coming back day after day, prayer that grounds itself in God’s promises and asks for his glory. It might be one honest sentence prayed every morning for a wayward child for twenty years. God is not impressed by eloquence. He hears the cry of his children.

In everyday life. Choose one thing you know is in line with God’s will, the salvation of a friend, the healing of a broken relationship, and pray for it earnestly every day. Write down the date you started, and keep looking at the horizon, like Elijah’s servant, for the small cloud.
verseByVerse.note: Elijah’s prayers are implied in 1 Kings; Jesus also gives the drought’s length as three and a half years.

verseByVerse.quote: My brothers, if anyone among you wanders from the truth and someone brings him back, let him know that whoever brings back a sinner from his wandering will save his soul from death and will cover a multitude of sins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If anyone wanders. The letter ends without benediction or greetings, on the subject of somebody else’s soul. The verb is to be led astray, the root of our word planet, the wandering star. It is drift, not a decision. Nobody announces that they are leaving.

Someone brings him back. That someone is very ordinary: not the elders, not an office, but anyone who notices and goes after him (Galatians 6:1).

Save his soul from death. Nothing higher could be said of one Christian going after another (Romans 6:23). God saves, but he uses believers as his instruments.

Cover a multitude of sins. It echoes Proverbs 10:12 (also 1 Peter 4:8). The covering is God’s work: the wanderer’s sins are forgiven when he returns.

Turned again. The word is the one Jesus used to Peter: “when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22:32). Peter wandered as far as a disciple can, and the risen Lord went after him by the lake, three questions for three denials (John 21:15–17). The Son of Man still seeks the lost (Luke 19:10) through the ordinary believer who knocks on a wanderer’s door.

Whose soul, and what death? The one who wanders is saved from eternal death by being brought back, and his many sins are covered by God’s forgiveness. Can a true believer wander so far as to be lost? Arminian Christians, who hold that a true believer can finally fall away, read the verse that way, and they do so out of a serious concern for holiness. The more likely reading is that the wanderer is either a believer whom God restores through the loving pursuit of others, or a professing member whose wandering would have shown that his faith was never real. Either way, the person who brings him back is God’s means of keeping him, which is why we must not leave wanderers alone.

What it does not mean. We do not save people by our own power, and the restorer does not earn forgiveness for his own sins; the sins covered are the wanderer’s.

A fitting last word. James has insisted that real faith shows in deeds, and that hearing is not doing. He ends with the most concrete act of love available to an ordinary Christian: noticing that someone has stopped coming, and going to find out why.

How do I approach someone who has drifted away? Go personally, not with a programme. Begin with friendship, not a lecture: a message, a coffee, an invitation to a meal. Tell them they are missed, and mean it. Listen more than you speak; there may be hurt, doubt, sin or simply busyness behind the drift, and you need to understand before you can help. Be honest, gently, about your concern for their soul when the time is right. Pray for them before and after. Do it in a spirit of gentleness, keeping watch on yourself (Galatians 6:1), and do not give up after one attempt. The shepherd went after the one sheep until he found it (Luke 15:4).

What if they do not want to come back? Then you have still done what love requires, and the result belongs to God. Keep praying for them, keep the door open, keep being their friend if they will let you, without pretending that all is well. Some come back after many years, often remembering the one person who did not give up on them. If there is serious unrepentant sin, the church’s elders may need to be involved, as Jesus taught (Matthew 18:15–17), always with the aim of restoration. You cannot force anyone home. You can make sure they know the way back is open, and that someone is watching for them.

For worship. The letter ends with a man going after a wanderer, because that is what God is like. “All we like sheep have gone astray” (Isaiah 53:6), and the Good Shepherd left the ninety-nine and came after us, over the mountains and into the dark, until he found us and laid us on his shoulders rejoicing. He did not merely cover a multitude of sins; he bore them in his body on the tree (1 Peter 2:24–25). Every time one believer goes after another, it is the Shepherd’s love walking out of the door again.
